utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you have a matter you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just very briefly. The next witness after Mr. Phillips is Mr. Coo, and I wanted to ask the Tribunal, bearing in mind that no decision has been made on the scope of testimony of Mr. Coo, that regardless of when the decision is made, the two give us notice, perhaps informally, about the gist of the decision because our cross-examination expectations range between five hours and five minutes depending on your decision. And I do believe that we need this in order to be able to prepare documents for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know which one we would prefer, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Ackerman has already suggested making written submissions where we initially anticipated dealing with this matter orally. Can you advance knowledge on that? Is there to be a written submission or are we to deal with it orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was filed late last night. CLSS has it. I have asked them to file it as quickly as possible this morning and that there is some urgency with respect to it, so I think you'll have it by 10.30 at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a joint submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand a number of think my colleagues are going to join it, and I don't think there will be any other submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the witness we are about to hear occupies the day, then later in the day we'll look at that written submission and we will probably be able to deal with it first thing tomorrow. If that means a brief gap while you regroup, then that can be arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think when you see it, Your Honour, you'll realise that looking at it might be a fairly intensive proposition because it is quite comprehensive. I think it's as much as 45 pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can tell you that we have spent a fairly significant time already looking at the latest version, and we may find that it may not take as long. We're not starting from square one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. That doesn't surprise me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you also have a matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unrelated to Mr. Coo, and I don't want to interrupt you when the witness is already in the courtroom, I have an objection to the use and tendering of Exhibit P632. It's an order that is not signed, not stamped, and there is no reference number. I think that this document has not been authenticated at all. It's been typed out. Nobody signed it. And at the beginning of the document, where there is a place for the reference number, there is no such number. So this is not in any logbook or anything. This is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to join in. I fail to understand the context in which two more documents are used, P928 and P1000, because I simply fail to understand what these documents have to do with the testimony of Michael Phillips. So this is all I have to say on this topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, can you deal with these, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, Mr. Stamp will be taking the witness. However, I can respond to the question, however. P1000 is making indications regarding the promotion of Pavkovic, and the use of the VJ within the interior of Kosovo that seemed to be against many of the statements made by the Serbian authorities to the KVM, amongst other international organisations. So it would be focusing primarily on the last few pages. As to P928, specifically on page 14 of it, there are some implications with regards to Sainovic's power over MUP forces and VJ forces, and we're focusing on those two aspects. Each have been admitted into evidence previously; however, those would be the two focal points we would be addressing with this witness in the event that the testimony requires it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does he have personal knowledge of the documents, or are you simply looking at these as something that has a bearing on the witness' evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they will be used in much the same way that P1000 was used with John Crosland when he testified, merely showing what the document is indicating is consistent with what he was seeing both in his meetings as well as what he saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your comment with P632?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We're foregoing that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think we have to look at these in the context in which they're raised in the course of examination of the witness, and Mr. Bakrac and you both have the assurance that P632 will not be used. I think we can now invite the witness into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we do, I think, for the record, I should indicate that the provider, the United States Government, is represented here in court by Ms. Denise Manning and Mr. William Horrigan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Phillips.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. I expect that you will be examined by a number of counsel here today. I can't tell you for sure how many. All I can tell you is that the first will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Phillips.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you starting by stating your full name.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My name is Colonel Michael D. Phillips.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. In November 1998, where were you posted and what was your occupation then?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: In November 1998, I was assigned at Pacific Command in Honolulu, Hawaii, and on the 4th of November I reported to Pristina in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In what capacity did you go to there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Working directly for Ambassador William Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what role did you have in relation to the work for Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I was his Chief of Staff, which encompassed working with our operations people in OSCE to develop operational strategies to deploy the OSCE verifiers into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what function that entailed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It entailed planning, it entailed strategy, it entailed working with the FRY and MUP liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have to carry out functions that involved observing events as they occurred on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did. We deployed to the field approximately three days a week to four days a week on the average.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long were you posted in Kosovo in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: From the 4th of November to about the 20th of March, upon the OSCE evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you deployed about three times a week to visit places in the field. Places like where? Can you give us an idea of where you would visit?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: To Malisevo, to Suva Reka, Podujevo, various locations where there was activity. Whether it be Serb activity, KLA activity, or MUP activity, we would try to go to those locations and observe the situation on the ground. And the purpose of those deployments was to look at the compliance of the OSCE agreement signed by Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic -- or agreed to by Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic. I don't think Mr. Milosevic signed the agreement, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a brief look at the Exhibit 658. This is the agreement on the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I won't trouble you to go through the document before us, Mr. Phillips. We already have it in evidence. But could we just have a look at a provision at page 2, the bottom of page 2, going on to page 3 in the English version. And the last sentence of page 2 indicates that: "The Kosovo Verification Mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify the maintenance of -- of the cease-fire by all elements. It will investigate a course of cease-fire violations. The mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times." Was that the purpose of your variation expeditions, observing activities in the field in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That was one of the purposes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you allowed free access during your mission in Kosovo? Did the situation remain the same at all times in terms of access?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes. We were not allowed unfettered access at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you explain that a little bit more. What was the situation when you arrived there, and did it change?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: When we arrived there, we generally had the freedom to move throughout Kosovo with little restriction. As the mission progressed into December 1998, January 1998, the restrictions on our travels became more pronounced by roadblocks, and it was often briefed to us by the Serbian police that the reason that there were roadblocks. And the reason we could not go to a particular village that we wanted to go to was they could not guarantee our safety, and therefore we were prohibited from moving around with unfettered access.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hold meetings with representatives of the Serbian government to try to iron out the issues that you had?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did, on several occasions, usually on a weekly basis. We would meet at the government building in Pristina with Serb officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were the senior Serb officials that you would meet with weekly?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicolae Sainovic, in Pristina; retired General Loncar; Mr. Lukic, who --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which Mr. Lukic is that? What is his first name, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall his first name, but he presented himself as the chief of the MUP or the commander of the MUP in Pristina. And there was an interpreter or two; Mr. Skoric was also present; and there was an interpreter, female, by the name of Gordana who was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the KVM, who would be present at that meeting, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker; DZ, who was our chief of operations, a British two-star general. I refer to him as "DZ." I cannot pronounce his full Polish surname. Ambassador Walker would have an interpreter with him, who was also a Serbian individual. Once in awhile we'd have one of the mission area coordination centre commanders with us from -- on occasion, depending on the incident that we were seeking help from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that these parties met approximately once a week. Did this frequency of meeting once a week continue right through your mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, what was the change, if you can tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: As we moved through the Podujevo time period, the December 25th period, 1998, up through the events leading to Racak in January, really after the Racak event, our meetings on a weekly basis ceased at that point. Leading up to that point, they were not comfortable meeting; they were hostile in nature, uncooperative in nature; and they begin to break apart from December 15th up through the middle of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in these meetings, about how many times was Mr. Sainovic present?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was present at each of the weekly meetings, with the exception of the final meeting just before the Racak incident. We'd ask to meet with him and could not contact him, and instead we met with Mr. Loncar. He met with us late in the evening of, I think it was, the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about how many meetings did you have with Mr. Lukic present?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was present at most of the meetings; certainly up through, I would say, all the meetings except the one at Racak on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The event at Racak was on the 15th of January. Does that affect your recollection of the date when you had this last meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying the meeting was after the event occurred at Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Racak occurred, and we asked to meet with Mr. Sainovic and we were unable to meet with him, could not be located; and, instead, we met late that evening on the 15th with Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the government building in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it the first meeting you had with Mr. Sainovic present. How was he introduced?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He introduced himself as a personal representative of Mr. Milosevic in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything about what his role was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He would be involved in all the political aspects and assist the OSCE in setting up its mission, and provide any assistance we needed to get the mission up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you first met with Mr. Lukic, how was he introduced to you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That he was the personal representative of Mr. Milosevic in Kosovo, as the chief of police, chief of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you -- did you come to an assessment of who was in charge of the Serb side that attended these meetings on the basis of what you observed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you observe that caused you to make this assessment?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, he was -- he sat at the table directly across from Mr. Walker. He did most of the talking. He gave guidance and direction to the other members on the other side of the table, to either lift a roadblock, allow access to a barracks. I mean, he was clearly in charge of providing guidance to his folks, left and right of him, at our conference table. And also of note was that none of his team would sit down until he sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he give you any undertakings in respect of how the KVM mission would be treated?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Early on we were told that he was there to assist us in any way that they could, and our very first meeting with him was quite good, I thought. It was upbeat. We felt we were not going to meet any cooperation problems or obstacles. In fact, I remember Mr. Loncar and Mr. Walker had known each other during their time in Eastern Slavonia. It was a very warm, friendly relationship. Mr. Walker was certainly upbeat, having seen an old friend again. And, of course, over time that turned out not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that, "turned out not to be the case"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, the relationship that Mr. Walker enjoyed with Mr. Loncar in Eastern Slavonia, per Mr. Walker to me, was the same relationship that he enjoyed in Kosovo with Mr. Loncar. It was more, I would say, uncooperative in its nature. It was a very defensive sort of relationship. Whenever the OSCE would bring issues to Mr. Loncar or to Mr. Sainovic, it was throughout the period of the OSCE deployment, and it just grew to be more uncooperative in its undertaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You told us just now that you were told that Mr. Sainovic was there to assist the KVM mission. Did he or anyone tell you what he would or could do to assist the mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, we were told that in order to allow the OSCE mission to come up to speed with the numbers, the number in the OSCE agreement was that 2.000 verifiers were going to be allowed to enter Kosovo; and to help expedite the deployment of those vary fires, they were going to set up a consulate office in Kosovo, Pristina proper, and that consulate never got established, even at the direction of Mr. Milosevic who at one time already said that it was established. It slowed the process of the verifiers coming into the country to execute the mission mandates of the agreement. So we did not find a cooperative nature of establishing that consulate to allow the verifiers to get in the country in a timely way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this the only situation, or were there other situations in which you were told that something would be done to facilitate your mission and it was not done?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: There were minefields that we had asked to be cleared so our verifiers could get to various locations in and around Kosovo, and we were on occasion told that they would look at that and clear those minefields so the safety of transportation to the verifiers could be guaranteed. The minefields were never cleared; they were never located and provided to us. We had asked for baseline information on the numbers of troops and numbers of police, numbers of weapons. We were never provided that baseline information. Just a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who did you ask for the baseline information and who told you that the minefields would be cleared?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We asked for the baseline information from Mr. Sainovic, from General Loncar, and from Mr. Milosevic himself, that we needed that baseline information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who told you that the minefields would be cleared?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic told us he would look into the minefields to see about getting those located and/or cleared so we had unfettered access in some of the regions. Our larger concern for the minefields being cleared was to bring the displaced Albanians back out of the hills to -- and get them back into their homes. So we were worried about the location of those minefields that had been planted along mountain passes and down in the valleys of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The failure on the part of the Serbian government side to live up to their undertakings or to cooperative, as you put it, based on your knowledge and observations in the field, was the failure due to an inability, a material inability, to effect those undertakings or to an absence of will to do so?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think it was an absence of will to do so. My observation of that situation was the more obstacles that were provided that the OSCE had to confront, it prohibited them from actually executing their mission and not able to undergo the evaluation of compliance of the agreement. It was an obstacle that was pretty obvious to us that was established to slow us down, because the mission, once the agreement was signed, moved very fast with fairly sizable numbers to bring them in. You know, the other obstacle was getting our cars registered so we could get the vehicles into Kosovo, to allow us to roam Kosovo with relative freedom. We couldn't get those -- those cars in on time as well. They were hindered at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I've been asked to pause by the stenographer. I would like us to bring up Exhibit 928.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would just like to look at one passage in Exhibit 928 and ask you one question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go to page 14 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are minutes of a meeting of the General Staff of the FRY. Now, I take it that you would not know about these meetings or this document. I just want to have a look at one part of the document and ask you how, if it does, would that bear on your experience of dealing with the Serbian government side, in particular Mr. Sainovic. One general is commenting that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not heard the witness say anything that might indicate that something like this should be put to him. I have not heard anything like that from this witness, what you're about to read now, that he said something in connection with this. If this is the broad context, the witness should say something about it and then this should be put to him to see if it corresponds to what the witness said. But I have not heard the witness say anything of the kind and for this reason I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we've heard evidence from the witness about a number of things and his assessment of what was going on. In anticipation, no doubt, of the Defence case, Mr. Stamp now wishes to put a part of this document to him to see how it fits with his experience on the ground. We see no objection to that course of action and we shall allow Mr. Stamp to proceed on that basis. Obviously, if he does something inappropriate in the course of doing so, we will hear from you further. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see here that one general is saying that, to quote: "I think it is a priority to ensure that not even Sainovic or any other Sainovic can solve these problems by lightly deciding to use the units," and he's referring here to army units. Does this accord or does this not accord with your assessment of Mr. Sainovic's authority in relation to the use of army units in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nor do I, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Fila, that question is not related to the evidence we've been hearing so far and I understand your objection. I think Mr. Stamp has to formulate another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you observed in meetings where Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Loncar were present that Mr. Sainovic would give directives in respect to how the activities of the Serbian forces should be conducted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And having regard to the passage I just read from that document, do you -- how does your experience of these meetings and what you saw occurring on the ground --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is not yet asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What you have just said was never stated by the witness. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the passage that you're highlighting is open to interpretation and it's open to us to compare that passage with what the witness has said. But asking the witness, in the way you are intending to do at the moment, to comment on this passage as somehow or other being equivalent or similar to his experience is not an appropriate question. It's not for him to make that judgement. Already -- I think you've already told us that this document is an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it is evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're highlighting a passage that you wish us to look at which we will in the context of the evidence the witness is giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll -- I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke earlier about displaced persons. Can you tell us briefly what was the situation in respect to the displaced persons that you observed within Kosovo during your time there on the mission.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: One example that I observed was in the village of Malisevo. It was a village that had been literally completely burned to the ground, and all of its residents had fled to the hills during the winter months. The town was besieged with heavy MUP activity, and one of my jobs was to work with the MUP and our liaison officers to try and get the MUP out of Malisevo, so we could bring back displaced people that lived in that village back to their homes before they froze to death in the mountains in the winter. And my recollection of that time-period, there were a couple thousand displaced people as a result of that village being attacked and burned and mortared. And one of our missions was to try and repopulate that village and rebuild that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this? When did you make your observation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This would have been in November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you bring to the attention those observations to the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It was presented to Mr. Sainovic, and it was presented to Mr. Milosevic, both in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the response and attitude of Mr. Sainovic, in particular, in respect to the issue of the IDPs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My observation of the response was that I would tell you that they were certainly concerned about the displaced people, but they also saw them as terrorists and was a village that while it had no Serbs in it or no Albanians in it was still heavily fortified with MUP police. And we couldn't understand what they were there for, what they were protecting, and what they were securing. There was no reason for them to be there, and Mr. Sainovic, I recollect, felt that it would be unsafe to pull the MUP out of there because terrorists, in his words, would filter back into the village and confront Serbian security forces once again. It was a key village, fairly close to Pristina. I think for the Serbian security authorities probably thought that that was a strategic location for them that needed to be secured, which is why the MUP stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall what, if anything, Mr. Sainovic said about the IDPs in general in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't recall anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your discussions with Mr. Sainovic, what language was used? Can you remember what language did he use?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He used both English and Serbian. He seemed to understand English well, although he had an interpreter there, but he seemed to have an understanding of English and spoke some English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he express himself in respect to the Albanian population in general in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, he certainly wasn't pleased with their activities from a perspective, as they referred to it, as terrorism --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Albanian population, Albanian people, did he say anything in your presence about Albanian people?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That they didn't belong in Kosovo that. It was the Serbian homeland and the cradle of Serbian civilisation, and felt that it belonged to the Serbian people and that the Albanian people had no desire to co-exist with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did he say that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: In one of our meetings in the November -- November time-frame in the early part of our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were attended also at various meetings in which Mr. Lukic was present. Based on what you observed, what was your assessment of his authority in relation to the forces -- armed forces in the FRY -- I beg your pardon, in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: What was his relationship with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was your assessment of his authority in respect to the armed forces in the FRY, in particular the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I'm not certain of his exact authorities, but I am certain that they had a relationship that was of a coordination-type relationship. From my observations in the field, the way the MUP and Serbian military forces worked together, there was clearly a relationship there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you also met with President Milosevic. About how many times did you meet with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I believe it was three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall a meeting on the 15th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I recall meeting on the 24th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: -- with Mr. Milosevic. And I believe the 15th of December was with Mr. Holbrooke and I believe General Clark, the best I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we pull up Exhibit 396, please. Could we move briefly to the next page and to the final page. No, no. The page before that where there's a signature, please. Could you go back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document before you -- well, do you know what it is? It's -- I shouldn't -- withdrawn. This is a letter dated the 23rd of November, 1998, signed by Ambassador William Walker, who proposed this letter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Walker signed the letter. I helped draft that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's addressed to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. Was this letter presented to President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you present at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This was in November, I believe, November 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Who else was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Which side?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Start with Mr. Milosevic's side.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was present, Mr. Sainovic was present, and Mr. Milutinovic was present. That's what I recall at that meeting. On were you side it was Ambassador Miles, Ambassador Walker, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, who arranged that meeting, and what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was we were having some trouble with cooperation, and Ambassador Walker felt it was necessary to deliver a letter in writing that outlined the nature of the agreement and the cooperation that we were looking for from the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the requests made in that letter, I think, speak for themselves, but how did Mr. Milosevic react to these requests that were made by Mr. Walker in the letter and verbally?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, he was very loud, upset that -- he felt that he was providing a high degree of cooperation. It was the view of the OSCE that he was not providing a high level of cooperation. We had asked for a number of things. We had asked for the consulate to be established. We asked for a medical evacuation helicopter by the Swiss. We had asked for body-guards to be armed. And while those wishes were entertained in Kosovo with Mr. Sainovic, they were later brought to Mr. Milosevic, and he felt that any security that we required would be provided by the MUP or the Serbian security forces. Any helicopter support that we required for medical evacuation would be provided by the FRY helicopter support. And that he claimed that the consulate was, in fact, established in Pristina and the fact was it never was established, so his information was wrong on that account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The letter indicates that action ought to be taken in respect to heavy weapons, check-points, observation points, police patrols, border security operations, and a variety of other matters. Were these, what I just mentioned, discussed at the meeting with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from your observations as to how the meeting was conducted and what was said, did you make an assessment as to who was responsible on the Serbian side for making decisions in respect to the use of the armed forces in Kosovo and who was responsible to implement decisions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I -- my observations told me that Mr. Milosevic was responsible for security force decisions, that Mr. Sainovic was to implement them in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said present at the meeting was also Mr. Milan Milutinovic. Where did he sit at that meeting in respect to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right next to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he say anything at that meeting, or did you observe anything about how the meeting was conducted on their side that led you to make an assessment as to his role?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic did not say very much. There was one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking about Mr. Milutinovic --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I'm backing to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. -- When he spoke to Milutinovic, it was never in English, although Mr. Milosevic spoke good English. So I never understood what was being said there; but after Mr. Milosevic would speak to Mr. Milutinovic they would have whatever discussion, which I didn't understand, and then Mr. Milutinovic would turn to Mr. Sainovic and say something. But I have no knowledge of what was being said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the basis for your assessment that Mr. Sainovic was responsible for implementing decisions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The basis of the decision was just the way Mr. Milosevic would lean over and speak. On occasion he would say that -- he would ask Mr. Sainovic to look into a situation for him. He would suggest to remove a roadblock, things of that nature. The OSCE often complained about roadblocks that prohibited them from getting into different villages and different areas to perform their mission; and when we brought that either to Mr. Milosevic or to Mr. Sainovic, clearly guidance was given from Mr. Milosevic for Mr. Sainovic to execute. Sometimes those roadblocks were removed quite promptly, other times they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on from that meeting in particular and speak about the meetings generally. Did you bring to the attention of the Serb side any complaints that you had from your observations in respect to the use of armed forces and the conduct of armed forces that -- the police and the army in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To which persons, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We brought that information to Mr. Sainovic in our weekly meetings and Mr. Milosevic in -- I don't recall exactly what meeting. I believe it was probably the third meeting with Mr. Milosevic; it would have been in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you brought those observation and complaints to Mr. Sainovic's attention at the weekly meeting, do you know where Mr. Lukic was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the -- of the Serb government officials, in particular Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: When we would bring forward the issue of excessive force as a result of KLA activities, it was -- their reaction was very defensive in nature, always pleading that they had to protect the Serbian people because the OSCE mission was not protecting the Serbian people. Our concern was -- was that the KLA was using small-calibre weapons in some cases, and there were MUP police officers that were killed by sniper fire. And the result of that would result in heavy Serbian or MUP combat action that was, in our view, of an excessive nature based on the result of the way that the KLA was going about their activities with -- with force. It was met -- the small-arms fire by the KLA was met with artillery rounds by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you elaborate a little bit more on what you mean when you say that their reaction was defensive, very defensive in nature.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Defensive in nature that the Serbian authorities, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Loncar, would claim that what they were doing was perfectly authorised. It was -- it made sense; it was a way that they had to respond to the terrorists that they were trying to defeat. They tried to justify their level of force as a retaliatory measure on the KLA activity, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The level of force which you just referred to, did you make actual observations of those forces in the field?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Did I personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think on the few occasions, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were these -- these units were from what parts of the armed forces, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, they were a mix. They were both MUP and the VJ. Podujevo was a good example of that kind of situation where small-arms fire from the KLA was met with heavy fire, tank fire, and that sort of thing, artillery rounds from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say that they were mixed. When you observed the forces in operation, did you make an observation as to the level of -- well, I don't want to ask a leading question. Let me ask you this: What do you mean when you say that they were mixed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Wherever the VJ was, the MUP were; wherever the MUP were, the VJ was nearby. I observed VJ and MUP talking together. I observed VJ repositioning MUP observation points and locations, Podujevo, one case in Malisevo. So that -- that's my observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's speak about Podujevo. When did you go to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Approximately December 25th, 1998, on Christmas Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The VJ had been up there for some time, for several days, conducting training activities, as we were told. They were very near Albanian-populated areas. It clearly was a KLA stronghold that they were looking at. The training, in my view, was kind of a way to deploy a large number of VJ troops and MUP to position up there. My observation was it was an attempt to draw fire and allow VJ and MUP action against the KLA in a particular stronghold that they had been located in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you observe if and how the VJ and the MUP operated together?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I remember one of the observation points where we had a VJ Serbian tank. Those men were dressed in green camouflage-type uniforms. The MUP was dressed in their typical blue uniform. The -- I'm not sure if he was a company commander, but the individual who was obviously in charge of that location for the VJ and the individual in charge for the MUP would converse and talk. That individual would go back and reposition some of his men as a result of that conversation. Our interpreters and myself were never allowed to be close to those conversations, but we would see the actions as a result of those conversations. And the MUP was located along the road leading up into Podujevo directing some of it traffic, some of it VJ vehicles. So there was kind of a -- certainly a command and control component to the MUP activity, and it appeared to me that the senior commander on site there the responsibilities belonged to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were at Podujevo, did you observe the MUP and the VJ or the VJ in contact with the civilian population there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: You mean the civilian population, both Serbian and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Albanian, Kosovar Albanian civilian population there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I did not observe Serbian authorities in contact with Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Did you take photographs of the armed personnel that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at Exhibit 2586. This is a series of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This one, this is the first photograph, and it's K0577160. What is depicted there? First, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It's a picture of a Podujevo, December time-frame, VJ and MUP. Obviously, this was a period of contact with the KLA, and I would tell you sometimes it was difficult to tell. There were blue uniforms and green uniforms. We felt that sometimes what we thought were MUP, the next day appeared as VJ in a different uniform, both in Pristina proper and at some locations of deployed sites. They appeared to be mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember what these persons in particular were doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We were receiving -- they were receiving small-arms fire from an apparent KLA stronghold, and they had just basically taken cover. And I remember, this was several years ago now, but if I remember they were trying to reposition forces to try to protect their own location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to the next photograph. Well, could we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whose writing is this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This is my writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is for the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go back to the writing. This is page K0577161.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This writing was ostensibly scanned in to have been -- to indicate that it was at the back of the photograph. Does this writing represent what it depicted in the photograph which you just saw?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No. The writing that belongs to the photograph that I wrote about was attributed to a woman whose husband had just been killed in front of his home, and she was leaving her home with two weapons on each shoulder, quite upset. And it's apparently been transcribed on the back of the wrong picture, but I know the photo because I remember very well the event that happened. It struck me as a very emotional event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does this look like a mistake in scanning this material into the system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, this is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's written on the wrong photograph by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I take it that what you've written relates to the death of a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to the next page; that's the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This depicts Serbian security forces down between these trees here, and they were taking small-arms fire from KLA stronghold. And the Serb forces were -- or entering this area to establish an observation point and firing points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you identify the Serb forces or the Serb force assets that you see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I believe the individuals on the ground were Serb. There was some MUP that were up there. As I say, it was several years ago, but there were Serb forces up there that were well-armed and certainly returning fire on the KLA side. I believe the APC carried out at the end is a MUP vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to the next photograph, please. Can we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is whose writing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This is my writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's K0577163. Does it describe what was -- what you saw in the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read it for us just to ensure that --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It says: "27 December 1998, Kosovo, shooting three kilometres west of Podujevo, Serb funeral convoy protected by militia or MUP on the road from Obranca to Podujevo." And by "militia," I'm referring to the MUP that were following the funeral convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we move on to the next photograph in that batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, who took that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I took that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It's a VJ location, VJ soldiers and equipment that they were deployed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And quickly, the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take this one?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I took this one as well, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what's in it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It's -- I can't remember if that was a tank or heavy artillery piece in there, but it was stuck, essentially, in the heavy mud and they had taken up position, had been there for some time with Serbian forces kneeling down because it was small-arms fire coming in their direction. I believe this also was up in Podujevo during December 1998 time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to the second photograph after the next, that is one P -- sorry, the one at page K0577167. Well, we are at 68. This is K0577167.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This was a -- a search of a -- it was a home of some type. I believe this was the Serbian police that were conducting this particular search, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It was near Podujevo, but not in Podujevo proper. Probably a couple kilometres. I refer to all these pictures as Podujevo because that's generally where we were that day and there was a lot of house-to-house searching going on because of the KLA activity located in the -- off of a hill up in Podujevo, kind of down in a valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. We have spoken about the coordination of the VJ and the MUP in respect to Podujevo, but can you tell us generally speaking from your field-work did you make any observation in respect to the timing, the timing of the deployments of the VJ forces in respect to the deployments of the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My observations stem from a couple of locations. As I walked to work, I had to walk by the VJ headquarters that was in Pristina; and in the morning I could see them -- vehicles parked outside the headquarters, heavy vehicles, APCs, small vehicles that were loading up troops and where the Pristina OSCE headquarters was located there was a MUP headquarters there and I could see and hear at the same time the MUP loading up into trucks and APC carriers and whatnot. Typically what I saw was the VJ would go out first, and then -- about 30 to 45 minutes ahead of the MUP and then the MUP would go out behind them in the same direction. And on occasion the OSCE verifiers tried to follow and sometimes we could follow and other times we couldn't, the roadblocks were such that we could not continue. Generally when we saw both components go there was some sort of trouble in one of the villages, there had been some shelling and some firing and some sort of exchange of fire would take place and of course part of our role was to make sure that the cease-fire stayed in effect. So we were, as verifiers, concerned about that and immediately tried to find out what the mission was, what their purpose of deploying out was, and we couldn't always get that answer in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go to -- well, I'll put it this way. On the 16th of January at about 7.00 in the morning did you go anywhere for observations, 16th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At about 7.00 Ambassador Walker and I arrived at Racak, in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect what we were just speaking about, the deployment of armed forces, what did you observe there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: When we arrived at Racak, we were called out by our centre commanders that were located in Stimlje, that there had been a fairly heavy exchange of gun-fire up on the village at Racak. And about 7.00 Ambassador Walker and I arrived, and there was several -- a lot of MUP on the road leading into Stimlje, throughout Stimlje, not much in Racak proper. And as we got into Racak we would see, behind us up on the hill-side, VJ, and they had been up there for themselves a few days conducting training. And we walked into the village of Racak, the first thing that we saw was a decapitated Albanian man in his late 60s, early 70s.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're into territory we don't need to enter, Mr. Stamp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last question I have about your observations at Racak. You said you saw - and I'm just speaking about what you said in respect to the forces acting together - you said you "could see VJ up on the hill behind us." What do you mean by VJ? What could you see? Could you just tell us what could you see when you say VJ, and what were they doing.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We could see tanks located up on the hill and artillery pieces up on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see them do anything?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: They didn't fire on the village while we were there, so I didn't actually see them fire, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you discussed with us earlier on several meetings that you attended at which Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Loncar was present. Based on what you observed in respect to the relationship between the two of them, did any one of them or both of them have any authority over the activities of the VJ in Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would tell you that Mr. Sainovic, whenever he was presented by the OSCE with the concern about Serbian security forces' behaviour, he would turn to Mr. Loncar or turn to Mr. Lukic and ask a question, What about that behaviour? So it implied to me he had some authority over those activities by the sorts of questions and concerns that he had, which each of those representatives from both the MUP, Mr. Loncar with the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, is the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I request that we take the break a little this morning -- can I request that we take an earlier break, that we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just to review the notes and some of the things that have arisen during this direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you any idea, at the worst, how long the cross-examination will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In total?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The trouble with breaking now is it knocks out the schedule so far as interpreters' breaks are concerned. As you know, we're tied in to these breaks. But if we're not going to need the last half-hour or so of the day, then it won't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my part, I think I have 30 to 40 minutes. Maybe if everybody else could give an estimate we'd know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll probably have a half an hour, Your Honour, but that again depends on Mr. -- I think we're going by order of the indictment for the cross. So it could be less, it could be more depending on the questions from the first two Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- sorry, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at probably at least an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment to think about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Phillips, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: In the meanwhile we save time. About the authority of Mr. Sainovic, you observed that whenever there was a question he looked at General Loncar and Mr. Lukic. He only looked or he expected a reply or he gave them instructions upon the complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would look and ask the question, What do you know about this, essentially, and/or give them guidance to find out why they weren't -- why the OSCE verifiers were not provided access to particular barracks. So he was inquisitive in getting the concerns we as the verifiers answered from either his MUP security commander or from his VJ liaison officer, which was Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No more than that? No reprimand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No directions? No orders to them, Do this, do that this way next time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes there were -- there was guidance provided what he needed to get an answer for but never a reprimand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. O'Sullivan. We'll take the break now. We have to have breaks at various stages, Mr. Phillips so that those who are working intensively behind the scenes get a chance to regroup and we have to take one of these just now. If you leave the courtroom with the usher he'll show you where to wait. It's very important that during these breaks you have no discussion with anyone. I mention this to you in particular because there are representatives of the provider of this material in court and it's important that you have no discussions in particular with them during any of the breaks. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 10.55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we'll proceed by the order of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, we received from the Prosecutor notes of an interview conducted between you and representatives of the Prosecutor's office in Washington, DC, between the 14th and the 16th of March, 2001. I'd like to ask you just a few questions about that. You sat down with two representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and is it correct to say that the interview was conducted on a question-and-answer basis, they would ask you questions and you would provide information you had in response to those questions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at the time in 2001, did you make your best efforts to be complete and provide information to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say and would you agree that your recollection of events was fresher and better in 2001 than it is today?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can make a judgement on that. I thought my interview with the Prosecutor in the month of March was probably better than my interview with the Prosecutors in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My question is a little different. I mean, with the passage of time- and there's nothing sinister about this- I'm just suggesting to you that your recollection in 2001 in which you experienced in 1998 and 1999, would probably be fresher and more accurate and better than it is today, eight years or nine years later. Would it be fair to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't make a judgement on whether it is or it isn't. I just remember what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Today in your testimony you claim that on 24th of November, 1998, you attended a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Walker, and Ambassador Miles. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is absolutely no account of that meeting on that date with these people in your 2001 interview. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: There was a meeting in November with Mr. Milosevic in 1998, I am pretty certain it was November 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were interviewed by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal last July, July 2006; correct? That's the information we have from them.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It could have been, I was interviewed a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Does that sound right, last year?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Roughly yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And we received a summary from that interview because we were not allowed to see the actual notes, and nowhere in that summary, nowhere in that summary from last year, do you mention a meeting on the 24th of November, 1998, with these six people including yourself. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that on November 24th there was a meeting, and whether I answered a question to that account during those interviews I can't recall, but I'm very certain of the meeting with Mr. Milosevic; would never forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On that day with those people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Pretty certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Pretty certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at the notes from March 2001 which we received from the Prosecutor, and on the 24th of November you said that you were having dinner in the government building of Pristina, and it was attended by Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Walker, Mr. Loncar, General DZ, and you. That's where you said you were on the 24th of November, 1998, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I certainly could have had that date wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that you have the meeting wrong and, in fact, my position is you never participated in the meeting where Mr. Milutinovic was present. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can tell you that I participated in a meeting in November where Mr. Milosevic was present; Mr. Sainovic was present; I'm certain Mr. Milutinovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You seem less than certain, sir, about Milutinovic being there.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly checking myself against the dates that you present to me. I want to be very accurate here, but to the best of my recollection that's the way it went down.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, tell me where and when, if it wasn't the 24th, which I say it's not, where and when did the meeting where you participated where Mr. Milutinovic was present, where and when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The meeting that I had with Mr. Milosevic that Ambassador Walker had with Mr. Milosevic and I was present was November 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you, give me the time and place -- or the date and place where you say you participated with the meeting with Mr. Milutinovic, because I say you never did.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't give you a date and a place. I know that I met with Mr. Milosevic in what was his white house, his building.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So you do not recall -- you cannot give me a recollection of a meeting that you had with Mr. Milutinovic; is it fair to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I never had a meeting with Mr. Milutinovic; I had a meeting with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. And Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: And I participated in the meeting. I didn't have the meeting. It wasn't my meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You participated. And I'm suggesting to you that you never participated in a meeting where Mr. Milutinovic was present. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the fourth time. THE WITNESS: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's asked and answered about three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's been answered very definitively, and I think it can be pursued by Mr. O'Sullivan if he wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you it's a possibility that he was not there. It's been eight years, like you said. My notes are what my notes say, and I relied on my notes at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. Phillips, from what we're hearing is your notes don't say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing my best to remember what happened in that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it doesn't help to fall back on the notes because they don't tell with this apparently, and that doesn't help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon -- good morning, Mr. Phillips, my name is Toma Fila and I represent Mr. Sainovic. I will be asking you some questions about your testimony today. You mentioned General Loncar and you said today that he was a retired general.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Defence Exhibit 2D9 to be shown to you. I'm sorry that we will be going through the same batch of exhibits all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So while we're waiting for this document, let me tell you that General Loncar was never a four-star general, as you indicated, and that he was a member of the coordination body of the federal government, the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So perhaps now you can have a look at the screen because the document has now appeared on it.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I see the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You can see here that this was signed by the president of the Yugoslav government, Momir Bulatovic. Does this correspond to what General Loncar was actually doing, I mean, the way it is described here in this document? Okay. We'll return to that later when we see where Sainovic was. But you said today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Fila, is a supplement to another one; is that correct? And the first 11 members of the commission appeared --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I will get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to me that the witness has said anything that really impacts on that document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I have to show him the previous document. Could we then look at 2D8. This is the document that actually precedes the one that we have on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please have a good look at this document. This document is the document that precedes the one we've just seen. So as you can see, this is a coordination body and its name is the Commission of the Federal Government for the Cooperation with the OSCE mission; and in a decision of the federal government - again, this decision is signed by the federal Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic - the members and the president, the chairman of this commission are appointed and the chairman of the commission is Mr. Nikola Sainovic. If you look at this document, you will see what the commission actually does. Please have a look at Article 2, Article 3; and if you look at the next page, you will see the signature and the date when this decision was actually made. As you can see, this is the 19th of October, 1998. It was signed by the Yugoslav Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic. Mr. Phillips, does this actually -- is it consistent with what you talked about regarding Nikola Sainovic's powers in Kosovo, saying that General Loncar was a member of this commission and that many others were on that commission, too?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't think I said that Mr. Loncar was a member of that commission. I'm not familiar with that commission, but I will tell you what I read here is consistent with what Mr. Sainovic was performing for OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That was, in fact, the gist of my question. So if you see that Loncar was a member of this commission, then you will agree with me that it is quite natural that the chairman of the commission outranks a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That makes sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of course. The next thing that I would like you to focus on is to see that this authority is given by the federal government and not by Slobodan Milosevic, who is not mentioned at all in this whole document, although he was the president at the time. But would you agree with me that this body, the coordination body, that is established by the Yugoslav government, that the chairman of this commission then is responsible to the Government of Yugoslavia? Does that make sense to you? And that is why he has to report to the Yugoslav government and to get his tasks from the Yugoslav government and relay them to you and so on. Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Naturally. So you will agree with me that when you say that Sainovic had to consult with somebody in Belgrade, that it did not refer only to Milosevic but the federal government because he had been appointed by them.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now let me ask you, when Mr. Stamp asked you a question, you said that Sainovic was Milosevic's personal envoy, you said that twice, and you said the same thing about Mr. Lukic. Does this indicate to you that Mr. Sainovic was not a personal envoy of anyone, but that he was there as a representative of the federal government, as the chairman of the Commission for the Cooperation. What does it mean to you, "personal envoy"? Do you think that all these people were personal envoys of Milosevic? If you do, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Sir, the only thing I can speak to on that is just how it was introduced to me at those initial meetings with Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Loncar, Mr. Lukic. I was introduced to them. They introduced themselves to us, and Ambassador Walker, as a personal representative of Mr. Milosevic. It is nothing more or nothing less than that. Right or wrong, or whatever it has to do with of the commission, that's just the way it was introduced to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you can see that this document does not really say that. Do you allow that what is stated in this document, that it is actually correct and that he was, in fact, a representative of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I certainly do believe that Mr. Sainovic was a representative of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. This may look to you as some kind of legal wrangling. You are an officer. It is much easier for your, but we have a saying that a general is worse than your mother-in-law. So that is why it is clear for us to be clear. You mentioned in one part of your statement Mr. Sainovic. Do you know where Mr. Sainovic was born?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't believe it was in Kosovo, but there was a discussion with Mr. Sainovic when we first met with him that his heart is in Kosovo and that he hangs his hat in Kosovo and that made the comment that he was born in Kosovo, but I understand that he was born in Serbia proper. But that was a discussion early on in him professing how much he loved Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I want to tell you, let me explain, in the notes in your 65 ter summary -- in fact, the notes from your interview in Washington, it is stated that you said that he was born in Kosovo and that he travelled to Kosovo every weekend because he missed it. This is stated in the notes that you -- that we have from one of your interviews. But I merely wanted to point out to you that he was born in Borovo, he was not born in Kosovo at all. He doesn't have any family there. I'm just trying to bring your attention to the fact that words are very important. He was in fact born in Bor.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can agree with you on that, sir, but as you say words are very important and I would tell you that I never said he came to Kosovo on the weekends because he missed it. I never said that anywhere in my notes or anywhere in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, it does in paragraph 1 of your notes, the notes from your interview in Washington. I don't want to use them as an exhibit, but that is what it says here. You can look at that. You have the heading, the first meeting with Sainovic, that's the last paragraph on page 2 and first paragraph on page 3. It says here that Sainovic knew Kosovo well because he had been born there. Somebody wrote that down. I see now that you say that you did not say that but this is what it says in the notes --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, you're misinterpreting me. I never said he missed Kosovo which is why he came back on the weekend. I'm referring to you -- I'm referring to you that he came to Kosovo Friday, Saturday, and Sunday to work with the OSCE mission, and I'm telling you that these are not my assessments or my assumptions where he was born; this is what I was told in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
