utterances.text: I agree with what you say today. I agree that this is, indeed, correct, but the notes contain something else. So what you're saying now, that's correct. So we don't have a problem here at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we do have a problem because the particular phrase you used is the one that the witness will not accept that he said and I certainly can't find it in the notes either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the notes made by people who interviewed him in Washington --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it doesn't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- On the 14th and 16th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't say in the one I've got, at least I haven't found it, that he travelled to Kosovo every weekend because he missed it. And it's these words alone that the witness is taking exception to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, okay, but this is immaterial. It says here that he was born in Kosovo Polje and so on and he was not. I simply wanted to stress how important words are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- That's why I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You resolved the problems you were concerned about and what you left trailing was a comment attributed to the witness which he did not make and that has also now been clarified so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the 9th of December, 1998, you had a meeting with Mr. Sainovic. If you recall, can you tell me whether the following is correct, that Sainovic suggested on that occasion that the Kosovo Verification Mission should use the entire Serbian health care system. It's on page 4 of your notes. The heading is: "Meeting with Sainovic on the 9th of December."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to my notes on that, but was that in my 2001 or my 2006 deposition or interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the 2001 document I think, page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I look at my notes here, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My "notes," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interview in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is -- who made --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll show it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Who made this record of the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a record that was done at the US State Department in 2001. It would have been -- the OTP at the time would have been Mr. Milbert Shin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you happy, Mr. Fila, that the witness refers to that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I have no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You may refer to it if -- or do you not have a copy in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got a copy, sir, it may take me a few minutes to find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- This -- may I just consult with my colleague? [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You say it was page 4, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just -- if we are going to refer the witness to that part of the interview notes but, could it be done in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These -- the interview notes themselves were not made available for disclosure to the public at large. They were -- the disclosure of these notes was restricted to use by the Defence if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's not even -- hold on. It's not the Defence that are using them, it's the witness that wants to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no need for this to be on a screen where it's going to be publicised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I ask if we are going to refer to it in the sense where we are reading from it then it be done in closed session. But my friend is indicating that we won't be reading from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All that's happened here, as I understand it, is that the witness has sought leave to refer to the document so he gives an accurate answer. I don't think Mr. Fila proposes reading from it. So let's see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, sir, I found the statement that you're referring to and you're asking me is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The statement -- the statement is -- is accurate and is a result of us asking for Swiss medevac helicopters, and the reply was that our medical health care system here in Kosovo is good and you should be able to use that with great trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Keep your notes in front of you. Would you agree with me that on that occasion Sainovic offered Mr. Walker escorts or body-guards from the Serbian MUP, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall that and he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that Mr. Sainovic offered Serb helicopters for the purpose of medical assistance to members of the verification mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Today you said that you discussed this issue with Milosevic and that he issued the definite decision, that it was actually he who made the decisions on the consulates, helicopters, and so on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think he was facilitating those decisions on behalf, which, as the commission states, was part of his mandate for logistics and support for OSCE, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You won't need your notes any longer. I don't need them to be read out, and I don't want to use them as an exhibit. Simply -- it was simply to jog your memory. Did you meet Mr. Ciaglinski, a lieutenant-colonel who testified here?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I know him, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On page 6890, lines 17 to 24, Mr. Ciaglinski said that the Kosovo Verification Mission, and I quote: "Could not use a helicopter similar to those used by the Army of Yugoslavia to attack the KLA, which was a well-known model. It's true that we were offered it, but we were unable to accept it for reasons of our security and safety, as well as the security and safety of our verifiers. It's very difficult to tell when it's a foggy day whether the helicopter had a white cross on it or whether it's being used to attack." So would you accept this assessment made by Lieutenant-Colonel Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Another witness, General Maisonneuve, testified here on -- on page 11085, lines 21 to 24, and page 10086 [as interpreted], lines 3 to 4; that's the testimony of the 3rd of March, 2007, where said that he had two men in his security who were Albanians and who told him they were about to join the KLA. I don't know how many Albanians were in your security there, but would you accept it was logical for Yugoslavia to agree that such persons should not be issued with weapons, I mean, persons who were Albanians and who wanted to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It's logical to me that I would not want to issue weapons to members who wanted to join the KLA, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. At one point you said that the request of the Kosovo Verification Mission for visa facilitation had not been accommodated, and there are various things here that you told Mr. Sainovic. But don't you think it's logical, in view of the structure that you stated, that as the president of the coordinating body for cooperation with you, he could only transmit those requests to Belgrade. This has to do with consulates, visas, cars, and the other problems you had. In other words, would you agree with me that Sainovic could not solve these problems personally when you complained to him about them, and that that's why the replies arrived only a few days afterwards? I don't know if I eve been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't know if he could have solved them personally, but he was certainly the individual who told us that we would have those made available to us, have the consulate made available to us to expedite the visas for the verifiers arriving into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And then Mr. Walker's letter was sent to Mr. Milosevic with the same request. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you expected Milosevic to be able to deal with this issue rather than Sainovic; otherwise, you wouldn't have written the letter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We wrote the letter because we weren't getting any action and our verification team was slow to arrive, and we were looking for a more expeditious manner of cooperation to get that consulate established.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But why did you apply to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Because we were not getting any action from Mr. Sainovic or in Kosovo from any other source. We highlighted this to Mr. Milosevic as an area of support we required, and -- because nothing was happening to our request to the personal representative, in this case was Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you expected Milosevic to solve this; is that correct? He was the only one who could solve it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We did expect him to be able to solve it, yes, and he told us that it was already established. So we assumed he had solved it, but in fact it was never established.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When answering questions from His Honour and from Mr. Stamp, you said that when you spoke at those weekly meetings if the problem had to do with the army, Sainovic would look at Loncar; if it was about the MUP, he would look at someone else. Let's first clarify one point. Apart from these weekly meetings, did your representatives have daily meetings with Colonel Kotur, for example, and other officers, the MUP and the army, lower level?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I was not present at those meetings. I understood they took place with our liaison officers because they did report back to Mr. Walker regularly, so I can assume that they did have those daily meetings at those levels, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you saw now regarding Mr. Sainovic's powers as the head of the commission, if he were to ask Loncar as the representative of the army or someone else who was in charge of the MUP, he had to cooperate with them to solve the problems that you were facing. When you said you had a military problem, he would look at the person in charge of military matters because he was evidently not kept up-to-date on that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow on from what His Honour Judge Chowhan asked you. Wouldn't it be logical that if there was the president of a commission who was supposed to help you and you presented a problem at the weekly meeting that had to do either with the army or with the MUP, for him to ask the army what the problem was about or for him to ask the police what the problem was about because that was what he was supposed to be doing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It would make sense that he would ask the army or the police what was happening, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was trying to get at, because the information, of course, was crucial for cooperation with you. How could he cooperate with you if he had no idea what was going on. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It is my observation and opinion that Mr. Sainovic knew full well what was going on in Kosovo. That's the only way I can answer that were -- certainly he knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And he received the information from representatives of the army, the MUP, the politicians, and so on, because that was actually his job description, wasn't it, as the president of the commission, to be informed about all this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't speak to what his job entailed. I see the commission was established. I see his position in there, but I don't know what the flow of information was for him or who reported to him or how all that was put together there. All I can speak to is the issues we brought before him to be solved in our weekly meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then he would look at one or the other of them and receive information from them, that's how you described it, whether Loncar or the MUP or whatever. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For example, when we wanted to visit a barrack, we couldn't get into the barracks. We would bring that problem back to that meeting, and he would turn to Mr. Milosevic and ask, Why couldn't they get into the barracks -- or turn to Mr. Loncar, Why couldn't they get into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sainovic would turn to Mr. Loncar and ask, Why couldn't you get into the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. You mentioned Malisevo and the problems concerning Malisevo. Would you agree with me that the problem of Malisevo was resolved on the basis of a joint initiative of the SRJ and the Kosovo Verification Mission, and it was solved by reducing the number of members of the MUP and strengthening or stepping up the numbers of the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission in Malisevo. This helped to defuse tension and enable people to return. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware, because this has been mentioned by others, that Sainovic advocated personally that this same model be applied in other places in Kosovo because it proved to be successful? Mr. Petritsch mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall any discussion on that example. I would tell you that Mr. Sainovic was helpful to try and get the Malisevo problem solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, remind me what you're referring to by the SRJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia. It's hard for us, too, Your Honours, to remember what our name is. Every time we go home, we find we are smaller and our name has changed. So when I come back from this trial, I don't know what the name will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's usually translated as FRY, of course, but you've clarified it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could we now deal with your personal notes very briefly. We'll start with your dinner with Mr. Sainovic on the 24th of November, 1998. Do you need to have the notes before you, or do you want me to put them on the screen? Very well. Let's -- no. Let's look at 2D17, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, hold on, Mr. Fila. What is 2D17?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be extracting a single sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. These notes are obviously downloaded into the system. Does your point apply to them as it applied to the interview notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Some parts of them, Your Honour. We would have to deal with them on a case-by-case basis, but this one is not one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you would have to be careful, Mr. Fila, to ensure that the ones that are put on the screen are not subject to any Rule 70 restriction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are just two sentences, and they are not subject to such restrictions. Could we please take a look at 2D17. Your Honours, the Prosecutor has all this. If they wish, at any point, to go into closed session, then that's no problem. Could this be shown, please. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In this exhibit there is a question. Mr. Walker asks Sainovic why there are fewer Albanians who want to live in Yugoslavia, and Mr. Sainovic says most of the people in Kosovo believe they can arrive at a political solution. This is what I wanted to show you. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is the following. In this passage, does it go to show what I believe it can show that Mr. Sainovic was in favour of a political solution, because he said that the greater part of the people in Kosovo believed they can arrive at a political solution. Would that show his being in favour of a political solution? That's what I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Sir, in all due respect, I can't make a judgement on what Mr. Sainovic was thinking here. I just recorded the moment of his comments, you know, his words, "The greater part of the people in Kosovo believe they can arrive at a political solution." What that tells me is that he was hopeful that there could be some sort of a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next thing I wanted to show you - and if Mr. Stamp feels we have to move into closed session, we will - that's 2D18, a meeting with Mr. Sainovic on the 9th of December, 1998. In e-court it's page 12 -- 1 and 2. I don't think it falls under Rule 70, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just continue with this one, Mr. Fila. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please find it, and Sainovic says here that security is the primary concern and that details should be discussed. It has to do with your security, and it deals with health care and making a list of joint efforts to ensure the best possible health care. These are your notes, and later I'll put questions to you about them. And then it says that the best possible solution should be offered, and that an entire system was on offer from helicopters to the entire hospital system. He says, "We're ready to offer this tomorrow in Pristina, Prizren, Pec under all weather conditions. We can offer you better than one helicopter in unfamiliar terrain. Our doctors can come and visit any hospital and exchange information on health care, so let's organise the best possible plan." And then he goes on to say: "I appreciate your honest discussion. Let's ensure the best possible health care system. There is a potential risk in flying in all weather conditions. We can give you a medical plane that can fly you to Germany, England, or other places; if not, let's discuss this."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now I have a brief question for you. Would you have noted, could this be construed as the wish by the Yugoslav side or Mr. Sainovic to find a solution to providing assistance, medical assistance, to members of the KV, that Sainovic is flexible because he really wants this thing to be solved? Would you agree with me now that I have read back to you what you have noted?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, sir, and forgive me, I know you read an awful lot there, but I'm not sure of the question you want me to answer. If you're asking me if Mr. Sainovic was making a concerted effort --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The offer, the offer.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah, the offer is absolutely correct. I remember that conversation. Mr. Sainovic was offering many things from the FRY, and our problem with being able to accept it was security. We felt that it would jeopardise both the FRY -- or the Serbian people and would jeopardise the safety of KVM as well, if we accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this a sincere offer, in your view? This is what I would like to know. When Sainovic offered you all this, was he sincere? Did he really want the problem to be solved, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I believe he was sincere and I believe he did want it to be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. In the same conversation, and now we're talking about Exhibit Number 2D18, the same exhibit, Sainovic said that the Ambassador Miles [as interpreted] and the head of the US-DOM were prepared to establish a constant presence and I was told of people coming back. This pressure cannot go on for more than two weeks because they will be dissolving. General DZ -- but the mayor of Malisevo said that the presence of international KDOM would give him confidence to bring his people back and also keep the force safe. And finally Sainovic says: "With joint efforts we can make a difference in the most difficult of situations."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page, please. Turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have read this out because it arises from this that both you and Sainovic, i.e., the government of Serbia or Yugoslavia, believe that the solution to the problem of Malisevo could be found in the cooperation between the international factors and Yugoslavia and that this could be achieved by the reduction of the MUP presence and the stepping-up of the international presence. And this is precisely what Sainovic suggested, that was his proposal?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't disagree with his proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You also stated that Sainovic reacted because of the funds from western Europe that were used to procure KLA with weapons, but according to his knowledge those funds had been defrosted, they were frozen, but -- and you can find it on the same page of the same document. And then Mr. Walker said this: "I will speak to the international community about preventing the purchase of arms. Bank assets need to be refrozen and Mr. Walker says also: "I don't want the KLA buying more better weapons. I will do something about this." And he also says: "Money, arms, people cannot happen without organised support. We will do everything in our power to stop the flow of arms. It is not in our interest to arm the KLA, despite statements in the press about President Clinton wanting to topple Milosevic. I will do what I can to find out about this." Do you and Mr. Walker adhere by the statement that western money was used to arm the KLA and that this wasn't good? So do you still agree what you noted on that day, because this is very important for our Defence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with the notes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your next note there's a meeting with Mr. Sainovic on 18 December, 1998. This is Exhibit 2D19, e-court page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Mr. Stamp has to say to this. Okay. So we can still remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Byrnes said this. Did you find it? Do you have it on e-court. Let's just wait for a moment until the document is brought up on the screen. Do you see it now? Mr. Byrnes says, second page, he says this: "On police information, all is going well. However, we need information one day earlier: With respect to cooperation with police, I am very pleased it has been good." And the most important thing is this: "I have felt very secure with the MUP and protection of the Army of Yugoslavia." Do you agree with Colonel Byrnes, that he as the personal advisor, i.e., the head person of the KDOM, felt secure under the protection of the MUP and the Yugoslav Army and that he did not need any other protection or that you, as a whole, did not need any other protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's just the way that the question is phrased that I'm objecting to. I don't think he can comment on how Colonel Byrnes felt, but perhaps the question is really directed towards whether or not he is recording what Colonel Byrnes said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question is seeking the impression of the witness himself because it goes on to say that he did not need any other protection or that you as a whole did not need any other protection. So it's your impression of that situation that you're being asked to recount.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is Mr. Shaun Byrnes, not Colonel Byrnes because he was not a military man. Is this the same Byrnes that we are referring to? The only Byrnes that I know is Mr. Shaun Byrnes from the state department and you referred to him as a Colonel Byrnes. I don't know a Colonel Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Shaun Byrnes. I didn't say "colonel," I said Shaun Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The spelling of that name is B-y-r-n-e-s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I found this in your notes. You noted that whoever said that actually said it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not disputing that, I just want to make sure that I'm referring to the right individual as you place him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: In regards to his feelings on the MUP and VJ protection, I have no reason to dispute that he felt safe. I certainly -- you know, I was fairly accurate in my notes with him. I know he roamed Kosovo with his team before OSCE was established with little problem. I'm assuming that he felt safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in your notes we find the meeting on the 14th January 1999 with Mr. Sainovic. This is 2D20 page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this on e-court. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it says in this document -- can you find the place where Sainovic is speaking. He says: "Glad to be back at table; glad our people were present at VJ site; communications were good, trust was upgraded, nobody tried to test anybody, tensions were high, and we worked well together. If we cooperate we can do more. If we do more we'll have to do less and have fewer problems. "We are pulling forces out of Podujevo. "We need to protect the rights of civilians, they must have the freedom of movement, et cetera. Malisevo is a good example where KVM presence is making a big difference. A local police officer speaks both languages is in place there. We must now follow the Podujevo and Malisevo and Orahovac examples. Podujevo is a critical point now, and the security situation must be followed very closely. "We are trying to start new initiatives. I have met with Mr. Hill twice and went to Vienna once. Our foreign minister went to Spain. We are emphasising the importance of the political process. "In Podujevo, a lot of families left Kosovo. Only a political dialogue can take care of this. In both places the KLA and the VJ must seek a political solution. "We want to work on the main elements of agreement and, Mr. Walker answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Time for a question, Mr. Fila. There's no need to read all of this. If the witness confirms it's an accurate record, then we can read it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You will agree with me that these notes show that the atmosphere of the meeting was very good. This meeting took place after the soldiers were liberated, if you remember, and the Yugoslav side wanted to make up -- make the most of this opportunity to step-up the political dialogue. And Mr. Walker, as you can see, shares this evaluation to a large extent. Did this meeting show a sincere wish on part -- on the part of Sainovic to resolve the situation through a political dialogue, that political means should be used to deal with the issues?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My answer has got some complexity to it based on the timing, and I would like an opportunity to work through this for just a moment. This was on the 14th of January. This meeting was a rather warm meeting. There was some elation about getting the VJ released. A current underneath that was getting the KLA soldiers released. There was some particular concern by Mr. Sainovic not to want to link the release of the KLA of a fear to show weakness in the government and being easy on the terrorist situation there. If you recall, Racak occurred on the 15th of January, the next day, and our observation was that the Serbs needed to make a point, an example, at Racak that while we had release of the VJ that they would not be easy on the KLA and what have you. So, you know, coming nine days later, I believe, was the release of nine Albanians, nine KLA Albanians. But the two or actually linked, and so it was -- it was more complex than what the notes are explaining here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the notes show optimism that prevailed at that meeting, and there was optimism that there could be a political solution. I apologise. Not only that, but also that a political solution is the only possible solution. Isn't it true that this could be inferred from your notes, and that this was the atmosphere of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, finally, something you said when we spoke about Sainovic's place of birth, which is not important. You also spoke about what Kosovo is, and you also explained that in answering Mr. Stamp's questions. Based on everything you told us, based on Sainovic's behaviour, I would like to ask you whether you have maybe mixed something up. The Serbian position is that Kosovo is an integral part of Serbia, and I'm sure that Sainovic must have told you this because this is a fact. But what exactly did he tell you about the Albanian population that resides on Kosovo? Did he tell you that Kosovo did not belong only to Albanians, that it could not be independent? Would that be what Sainovic meant? Can you please try and recall what exactly he told you when he was speaking about finding a solution, a political solution, to the issue of Kosovo. And please try to make sure you use the right words because that's very important.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would tell you Mr. Sainovic was sincere about arriving at some sort of a co-existence strategy for both the Serbian population and the Albanian population to co-exist together. I hope that's clear enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Clear enough and I am very grateful, and I have no further questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm Norman Sepenuk, and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic. First of all, I don't think the record's clear what branch of the service you were in when you were serving as Chief of Staff for Ambassador Walker. Was it the air force?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the US Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And are you still a member of the US Air Force? Are you currently in active duty?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what's your current position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's not permitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that. Fine, I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you -- as I understand it, you were Chief of Staff to Ambassador Walker during the period that we're talking about, and that you kept substantially verbatim notes of meetings you had with the general -- with the ambassador and other people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And the notes covered a period -- what period? Just tell us the period covered by the notes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I had approximately ten notebooks that covered approximately October to July 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: October 1998 to July 3rd, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And we do have copies of your notebooks until February 18th, 1999, and they cut off after that. Is there any particular reason for that, that we don't have the remainder of your notebooks? There's a period of -- you say the notebooks went to what period, March?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I took notes up until I left the area after we evacuated, March 20th. There were a couple of notebooks that went missing. I know for one of certain and that was a notebook from the meetings with Mr. Milosevic. That notebook disappeared. I have no idea why, where, who, but I can't answer the question why they ended on February 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As far as you know, you did take notes during the period February 18th through March 20th?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The date of the meeting that you say a note -- of the notebook has gone missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of my meetings with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly which one. I want to say, sir, it was a December piece, but one of the notebooks I had was gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There is this one-month period that we don't have and perhaps the Prosecution at the break we can confer about it because I'm not sure why we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know why either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Unless there's an answer now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We've given everything we have. We collected the notebooks that he had available and we disclosed them under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If -- if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could tell you, sir, that there was a point where I ran out of paper and I was writing on the backs of maps and that sort of thing and certainly I would not turn those things over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Sepenuk, it's a matter you can raise with the Rule 70 provider, and if it emerges that there is other material and it's permissible to use it then we've indicated what action could be taken in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, Colonel, I would like to go over some of the entries you made in your notebooks and I'm going to speak very slowly so that if there is any problem at all with any of the entries, Mr. Stamp will have an opportunity to make that known and we can take care of that situation as it arises. So I'd like to start with the very early part of your notebook, that's an entry for November 14th, 1998, it's 3D545 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The difficulty now, Your Honours, is that it's impossible to determine whether or not the extract which Mr. Sepenuk wants to refer to is something that is permissible to be shown outside of this courtroom because he has just put in the exhibit a whole batch of material. It is not restricted to a page or two pages that is relevant, as was done by the previous cross-examiner --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact this is -- this is about three lines on one page --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we have about 30 pages for that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, but I excerpted only one very small part of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The problem is that that is not what is going to be in e-court as an exhibit and e-court will have a whole batch of pages which could involve telephone numbers, material which clearly could not be published outside of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a way of dealing with it if you just hold on for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The exhibits that have been used so far have not be shown on the feed to the public, and therefore there is no risk that inadvertently something will appear on a public screen. And if counsel does as he has said he will do, which is deal with each one slowly, you will have an opportunity of directing our attention to anything that should not be exhibited. He started by referring there to the date, and that would normally be some guide, I imagine, to whether it is something that ought not to be exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it's 3D545 and to make it more specific it's 3D01-2880. That's the specific page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this purports to be a discussion with Ambassador Hill and tell us briefly who Ambassador Hill was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Hill --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before, can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Colonel, just briefly, who was Ambassador Hill?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: At the time he was the ambassador to Macedonia, and also -- I guess the best way to describe him was kind of a Special Envoy for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he was active, was he not, at the time in trying to get the Serb forces and the KLA together and work out some sort of an agreement or at least the Serbian government --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And again, you are taking notes about this meeting. You are there with Ambassador Hill and with Ambassador Walker; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And in this excerpt you say: "The KLA wants to dominate the political landscape and use guns to do it." And who said that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Hill said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And were you aware that the KLA had threatened to kill anyone who signed any agreement sponsored by Ambassador Hill. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics. I remember something about it. I wouldn't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General DZ actually submitted a statement in which he stated that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah, it sounds familiar to me. I can't be precise but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't dispute it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And again in your notebook, 3D545, page number is 3D01-2885, a very short excerpt again. And I'll pause here in case there's any problem. Where you stated, and again this is Ambassador Walker speaking, and it says: "Assertive verification is the right turn for KVM -- not monitoring." And do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I recall that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And do you -- what did Ambassador Walker mean, to the best of your knowledge since you worked so closely together, by the term "assertive verification"? What was he getting at there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He wanted his verifiers to be aggressive in the sense of getting into the village, talking to people, talking to the mayors, talking to the leadership, to get a real ground truth of what was happening in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And speaking of assertive verification, do you count General Drewienkiewicz, General DZ, as someone who also subscribed to that view?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in your notes at 3D545, specific page number at the bottom 2901, which I refer you to, you said: "General" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we pause?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, please. Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you see that there in the second paragraph: "General DZ was a hard-nose, no-nonsense Brit." Have you picked that up, sir, second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I have, sir, but I've been asked to stand-by for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sepenuk, life's too short for us to proceed this way. The original order made was that reference to documentary material which had been disclosed confidentially would be made in closed session. You know how anxious we are to avoid closed session, but it may be that it's the only practical way of dealing with this without extending the session to double its normal length.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Unless I'm missing a point, this material seems absolutely benign to me. I don't understand what the problem is, frankly, but -- and perhaps the OTP can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it does, I think, fall within the category of confidential material, doesn't it? It was disclosed to you under Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It was disclosed under Rule 70, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's covered by the order if there's insistence upon it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the problem is that it's outside of the 65 ter summary so we have to check every time, but Your Honour has already addressed that. But we could do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know that it's open to us to review the transcript and make it public after the session is over, so I think to expedite this we shall go into closed session as long as Mr. Sepenuk is cross-examining on confidential material, and then we shall review the transcript with a view to making it public thereafter. We shall resume open session when we are no longer dealing with these confidential notes. [Closed session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So again, Colonel, directing your attention to that exhibit, second paragraph there, it says: "General DZ was a hard nose, no-nonsense Brit named as a deputy to Ambassador Walker's staff." Now, who was saying that? Is that you saying that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is that you saying that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, that is me saying this in these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Then you go further and saying: "DZ is a prickly sort of fellow, and works his staff to the bone; a very capable officer, but in want of a power position." Again, that's you speaking?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you found him to be a sort of "prickly sort of fellow"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was prickly, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that if you found him prickly, perhaps others like the Serb armed forces may also?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I certainly can't speak for them. I can only speak from my judgement, but he was a British two-star and wanted a position -- to be sure he owned a position of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, under the October 25th, 1998, Clark-Naumann-Milosevic Agreement, the army and the MUP forces were required to bring down their level of presence in Kosovo to levels preceding the outbreak of terrorist activities. Now, you do remember that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Could you just say that one more time, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Under that October 25th, 1998 agreement, you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's the Clark, Naumann, and President Milosevic also signed it. The Serb forces, army and MUP, were required to bring down their level of presence in Kosovo to the level which existed prior to the outbreak of terrorist activities, and that took place in February/March of 1998 [sic]. All I'm asking you is you recall that was required by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is vague to the extent that it is -- it joins two different issues, one is the question of terrorism; the witness accepting that the witness focussed on that or should the witness be focussing the level of Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: May I answer that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's right in Exhibit 395, the language is that the: "In order to further encourage the return to peace and normality, the state authorities of the FRY will bring down the level of presence and the equipment of security forces (MUP and VJ) throughout Kosmet to normal levels, i.e., to the levels preceding the outbreak of terrorist activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's one of these questions that possibly didn't need to be asked, which causes us so much controversy. Can we move to the question you really want to ask now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, the question is -- I have to ask him whether he was aware of that provision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that there were provisions that troop strengths had to be modified to pre-existing numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you also know, do you not, that the level of presence was reduced by MUP and VJ?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I cannot accurately answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't accurately answer that. I don't know because we never got a base-line of what the actual numbers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But don't you know that both the VJ and the MUP withdrew their forces from Kosovo in accordance with this agreement? You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I wouldn't tell you that I know that or don't know that. I can tell you that I don't have any information to corroborate whether they, in fact, reduced and pulled out to meet the numbers of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you know -- we have testimony from a number of people in this court, including General Naumann, who said that they did just that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Okay. I can only give you my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And do you know whether after that took place that the KLA just moved in and re-occupied those positions. Do you know that? We've also had testimony in this trial concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah. I know that the KLA did fill vacuums of departures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to refer you now to your notes 3D546, and before that I want to ask you that isn't it true that after the KLA filled this vacuum, as you put it, that most of the provocations from that time on came from the KLA side and not the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't give you an accurate answer on that. I don't have a way to balance the numbers. There were provocations on both sides, regardless of who filled the vacuum. The Serbian VJ filled a vacuum when they took out Malisevo, and they went in there. When some Serbs moved, troop rotation, KLA filled those vacuums, so there were provocative acts on both sides from my observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you can't say whether most of them came from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's examine your notebooks and see what your notebooks have to say on that subject. And 3D546, page number 2932; this is your notebook for 30 November 1998. We'll wait until it's up on the screen. And this is with a reporter for the New York Times named Mike O'Connor. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were you at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall. Let me just look at this for just a moment here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah. Why don't you scroll down so the colonel can see the date. That's it. Yeah. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, the comment there by Mr. Walker: "Most of the violent acts are being committed by the KLA ..." "Most of the violent acts" actually means being committed by the KLA are aimed as provocative acts. Mr. Walker said that statement a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That most of the violent acts were committed by the KLA. --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That most of the violent acts being committed the KLA are aimed as provocative acts, not most of the KLA as you state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's go a bit more slowly then. First of all, Mike O'Connor appears in these notes several times, not just one time, and you have no memory of talking to him, a reporter for the New York Times, who wrote a number of articles on the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: If you had any idea how many reporters that I dealt with or that came through OSCE, you would be overwhelmed. I don't remember Mr. O'Connor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you never read his articles, or did you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I didn't have time to read the paper when I was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, he was working on a story, according to your notes, describing the KLA moving closer into the areas that they had not been before. This is what we were talking about, that they were filling this vacuum, as you put it. And what do we do, and Ambassador Walker said,"We jaw-bone them." Right? That is what it says here, "Watch them, let them know the international community is watching. We jaw-bone them"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way, I have to ask you: When you were being questioned earlier by Mr. Stamp, you said when you were meeting with the Serbian officials and they were -- and I quote what you said earlier this morning. You said: "They were always pleading that they had to protect the Serbian people because the OSCE mission was not protecting the Serbian people." Now, that's true, isn't it? You were not protecting the Serbian people, were you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would disagree with that statement. We had a mandate to protect both sides, not just one side or the other, and both sides were equally important to Ambassador Walker. When Ambassador Walker -- and he spoke to jaw-boning on different occasions. He had an impact with the KLA leadership. They would listen to him, and they would put down weapons and move away from being provocateurs. So he was effective and that's why, I'm sure, he referred to Mr. O'Connor here, is the best way to deal with them is to jaw-bone them because you can't bomb them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So there were unarmed verifiers who could jaw-bone, but beyond trying to use persuasion that was the end of it, of course, with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Walker goes on to say: "Most of the violent acts are being committed by the KLA." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That's what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like you to look at your notebook 3D546, page 2954, entry for 4 December, 1998. This is with Secretary-General Solana, and who was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Secretary of NATO, general secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he apparently was having a meeting with Ambassador Walker -- or I should ask you that. Is that what was going on here?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on the next page, that would be 3D01-2955 and 3D546, there is a question. Oh, that's up. It says: "What is your feeling of the mission?" Now, who is asking that question, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I believe that would have been Mr. Solana asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It says: "We need the political settlement UCK/KLA attitude towards us sees KVM as a security-blanket." Now, who would have said that, Ambassador Walker would have said that?--

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what does he mean by that: "UCK sees KVM as a security-blanket"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: What he means by that is whenever the OSCE orange vehicles were in and around a KLA location, any activity by the VJ or the MUP essentially was nonexistent. So they felt safe when the orange vehicles were in the village or in and around their location.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And if you would look at the next exhibit which is 3D546 at page 20 -- it starts at page 2956, but I want to ask you about an entry on page 2962. And -- this is 4 December, 1998. NAC, what does that stand for, NAC with the secretary-general?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The NAC was a meeting of all the senior NATO officials. It was a high-level meeting. I can't recall the acronym I know what it was but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all right, it doesn't matter. And then Ambassador Walker address for 25 minutes. So I take it what follows then are the high points from the address of Ambassador Walker; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And on page 2962, which is the last page of this particular excerpt --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher will put that on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Where it says under extraction force. It says: "KLA is a provoking element. Milosevic has told his troops to show restraint. Some evidence to support this." Is that what Ambassador Walker was saying on 4 December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then on -- and I'm not sure we're going -- we're going to have to put this up. I'll just try and ask you this and see if your memory serves you well here, the next series of questions very brief. On 14 December 1998, the notebooks reflect and the record in fact reflects that 6 teenage Serbs were killed by the KLA at the Panda Bar in Pec. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then a few days later on December 17th, the Serb deputy mayor of Kosovo Polje was kidnapped and killed in Pec. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then on 30 December 1998, there is a meeting with (redacted) and (redacted). That's 3D549 and it starts at page 3068 if we could start there, and what I want to ask you about is a brief extract on page 3069. And that is -- no, I don't think that's it. It's 3D549, page 3068. Yes, that's it. That's a meeting with (redacted) (redacted), Colonel, and on the second page of that, if you just would put that up, please, 3069, it says: "Walker." Mr. Walker says, "The theme in the press among Serbs," and that's as of 30 December 1998, "the theme in the press among Serbs is we are not stopping the KLA actions. In fact, they are increasing." Is that what Ambassador Walker said?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I have to rely on my notes here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you to do. And along those lines about KLA acts, terrorist acts increasing, let's just pause here on Podujevo which is also toward the end of December and I'm not going to show you anything at least right now, Colonel, so you don't have to focus on the screen so much but in that period beginning around late December and extending into January we did have this problem, very serious problem, potential problem, in any event, in Podujevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you were there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Podujevo, as you will recall was a very important strategic location, correct? Certainly to the Serb forces? It was the location that connected traffic from Belgrade down to Podujevo to Pristina. It was a very important road, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Very important to the Serbs to keep it clear, both the Serb forces and for civilians in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that was also one of the areas, as I think you know, where this vacuum again was filled, in other words, the VJ and the MUP had been in the area a few months before off and on because of problems in the area, they were in, they retreated, they were in, they retreated, and the KLA again after the Milosevic-Clark Agreement had moved back into the area. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the people of the area were in fairly desperate straits. Do you remember that at all, the civilian population were essentially being driven out of the area by the KLA -- Serb civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah. The Albanians were being driven out as well, but the population as a whole was departing the area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And there were KLA acts of terror -- you don't disagree with this. KLA acts of terror in the area causing the flight of Serbian families?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: There was all kinds of actions by the KLA that was causing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. And to your knowledge, did these Serbian civilians or at least representatives of these Serbian civilians in the Podujevo Municipal Assembly request repeatedly the assistance of the MUP and the VJ to come in and protect them? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't remember it, but I don't dispute it though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't dispute it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's move on now in our narrative here to we're now at the end of 1998, and we're talking about increasing KLA provocations and attacks. So we'll move into January of 1999, and, again, I'll ask you if you can rely on your memory. If you can't, we can put these up on the board, but you might be able to remember this. Do you remember on January 8th, 1999, there was a KLA ambush of a MUP patrol near Stimlje and Suva Reka with two MUP soldiers being killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Vaguely. But I know that there were -- there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If I represent to you --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: -- MUP fatalities down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If I represent to you that that's exactly what happened, will you take my word for it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This way we don't have to go to the screen and all that stuff?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then on January 9th, there was a KLA ambush south of Pec, ten kilometres south-east of Pec, MUP convoy of at least a hundred. Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: An ambush where a hundred --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There was a convoy of a hundred, but it was a KLA ambush, yes or no, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine. On January 10th, 1999, the KLA conducted another ambush near Pec and killed one MUP, and maybe we should go to Exhibit 3D550.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, can I ask you the purpose of this cross-examination of this particular witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He's saying that he doesn't recall, doesn't know, whether the -- most of the KLA -- most of the provocations came from the KLA side. The allegation, Your Honour, is that excessive force was used; that was part of his direct testimony. Our position in this case throughout has been most of the provocations - and there's been testimony on this - most of the provocations came from the KLA throughout Kosovo, and that these six men sitting behind me were absolutely justified in being afraid of the KLA and responding to these provocative acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that, but what I don't follow is how this exercise, asking a witness about matters he doesn't know anything about, helps to make any progress on your point whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He does know about it, Your Honour. His notes are a contemporary reflection of events. It's better than a memory, because he says right in his notebook. He bears out what our argument is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was just concerned that the two events on the 8th and 9th of January he knew nothing know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine, and I will move on. He did say that he would concede the ambush. We've had testimony on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He said he wouldn't dispute it, but that doesn't give you any evidence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We've had testimony, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, there's plenty of other testimony about these things, but I just want to be sure that what your are doing is necessary in relation to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I feel it's absolutely necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think is our time anyway for the next break, and we shall break now and resume at quarter to 2.00. Could you again leave the courtroom, Mr. Phillips, with the usher, and we will see you again at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to place on the record the position of the Rule 70 providers in respect to the cross-examination, the line of cross-examination that has been pursued by my friend Mr. Sepenuk and also my friend Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just a second. Mr. Phillips, there's obviously a legal issue to be dealt with here. I'm sorry you've been brought in. I didn't know this was going to happen. Could you leave the courtroom, again, while this is dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's really a matter of principle. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- order of the Trial Chamber permitting the testimony of this witness allowed certain conditions, and that is that cross-examination be restricted to the content itself, but I think we could say the scope of the rule 65 ter summary and might I add that it goes towards credibility. The cross-examination has gone well beyond the order of the Court limiting the areas that were subject to cross-examination, and the order did envisage that the cross-examining party may request the Rule 70 provider to lift the restrictions in respect to certain items that they think might help their case. No request has been made. I just wish to put that on the record. So the Rule 70 providers are placed in the inviduous position of having two make decisions by two representatives who are here in court and not by the government itself as a whole, prior to the witness testifying. So the main point is that the cross-examination is outside of the order restricting the areas that it may cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me some examples of that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The questions that were being asked in respect to certain events that happened in January where Serbs might have been killed; questions that were asked in respect to conversations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's take them one at a time. The first one is January questions about, what do you say, the killing of Serbs. That was the 8th, 9th, and we were about to go on to the 10th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you would say that it's an order for Mr. Phillips to express a view that the Serbs were using excess force, but counsel can't cross-examine on the activities of the KLA to make the point that it was proportionate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The point I make is that the cross-examine -- the order of the Court narrowed the areas of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But these are the same areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A question, it is my submission, about the events in January in which some Serb civilians might have been killed does not fall within the evidence of the witness as effective in the 65 ter summaries. The witness might have said there were excessive force, but the two are not logically related. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What? The activity of the KLA is not related to the use of excessive force by --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying the activity of the KLA is not related to the use of excessive force. My submission is that questions about persons, civilians who might have been killed at certain times, go beyond the scope of his evidence about the use of heavy artillery by the Yugoslav Army in response to small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you would say that he can't ask about a KLA attack on a convoy of a hundred?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which is one of the two issues, I think, on either the 8th or the 9th of January. He can't ask anything about that to suggest that the threat from the KLA was one that merited the use of artillery? Whether you and I agree with it's quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And whether it makes sense is quite another matter, but surely the two things are intimately related, and the one is simply cross-examination on the use of excessive force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, in respect to the question about the convoy, there might be a relation to the evidence of the witness in the Rule 65 ter summary. But it could never be within the scope of his examination or the 65 ter summary to ask him questions about every -- about any allegation of a Serb civilian being killed by the KLA. There was another line of questioning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that is outside the scope in respect to an interview that Mr. Walker had with a reporter. The line of questioning in respect to what General DZ said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you would say that a statement by Walker that most of the violent acts are being committed by the KLA is not a legitimate field of cross-examination on the issue of the use of excessive force by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he's the head of the mission, monitoring the activities of both sides, and you would say that that was not legitimate cross-examination on the issue of excessive force?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would agree that it might well be legitimate cross-examination if the Defence abided by the rules by requesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. They're allowed to cross-examine on the areas covered in examination-in-chief, but you're saying that that cross-examination is not an attack on the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is my submission that that area would not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, our only remedy here, if we don't agree with you, is to terminate the evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was about to move on. We do not -- we do not seek sanctions. I raise it to put it on the record because there are issues that might affect other witnesses. The Court made an order that the cross-examination must be within the framework of the Rule 65 ter summary, and the representatives here are forced in the invidious position not having been notified prior to the cross-examination as the order envisaged of having to make decisions on the spot. So what is happening here is that we do not seek sanctions because we are trying to cooperate with the Defence, and we are trying to have the evidence heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're not objecting to any of the cross-examination that's taken place so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We reserve the right to object, Your Honour. We place on the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we've heard the evidence. You're either objecting to things or you're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just placing on the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, this fancy footwork, Mr. Stamp, is not the way a public trial should be conducted. The Rules should be clear and you addressed it that way initially on the basis that the rules been broken, and that's the Court's responsibility and we're quite happy to take on that issue. But let's be clear one way or the other what is it you want done?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The least we would expect of the Defence is that they were required to act with restraint to conduct the cross-examination with restraint in respect to matters that are outside the scope. They ought to have requested the permission of the Rule 70 provider to enter into material that is outside of the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the comment -- the third matter you said was something about what DZ said, or was it just Mr. Phillips' view of DZ that was the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That he was a prickly individual and a hard-nosed - was he described as? - no-nonsense British officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That again may appear innocuous. But as innocuous as it is, the question is in breach of the order. It is a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't accept that any cross-examination about the conduct of members of the KVM goes beyond the examination-in-chief; that would be your position again?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
