utterances.text: Not any cross-examination. Cross-examination about conduct which is not subject -- which is not a topic within the confines of the Rule 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what are you asking us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this point, as I indicated, we reserve the right to be at liberty to object in the future to the Defence asking questions in breach of the Court order, but we would also ask through the Court if the Defence could be restrains from asking questions that not in the terms of the 65 ter summary. It is, as I indicated, in a spirit of cooperation that we have tried to make decisions on the spot, but I hope that the Court understands that it places the provider -- the provider is a country. It is a government of a country, and it is a difficult position to be making decisions in court; whereas, the Defence had the opportunity of seeking and probably obtaining permission from the provider to go outside of the materials, the matters, set out in the 65 ter summary. May it please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the avoidance of doubt, Mr. Stamp, the order is that cross-examination shall be limited to the scope of the examination-in-chief and the matters affecting the credibility of the witnesses. It's scope of the examination-in-chief that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we may differ on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, before the Court deliberates, add that one request we do make is that the Defence be required to enumerate now any matter beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief which they intend to ask about; and, secondly, the -- I would like to note on the record that what is being used is a document that was disclosed -- what is being , primarily, and that is the notebook that was subject to Rule 70 and, therefore, even if it is used any part that is used, we would request that it be sealed under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that -- I think that particular rule that the material should be admitted under seal applied to all the exhibits in this case, but there was some doubt earlier and I understand was told by someone on the Defence side that these were not the subject of the Rule 70. In fact, Mr. Fila, I think, told me that this was not the subject of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right, well I wasn't to know that, I think, because I think this was disclosed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I indicated that by -- to Mr. Fila, but I indicated it without advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you have the assistance of representatives of the Rule 70 provider in court so you're quite well-equipped today, and it's for you in these circumstances to take objection to any questions which you consider go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. We are, as a Bench, unanimously of the view that none of the questions you've identified do go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief; and therefore, that issue will have to be addressed if you continue to hold that view in relation to any similar issues that are now raised in cross-examination. And this may well undermine this evidence completely so far as the Trial Chamber is concerned. We may have to simply abandon the exercise if there is insistence from the provider that questions which we think are perfectly legitimate cannot be asked. But we will have to review that situation as and when it arises. I'm also happy on behalf of all of us again to invite the Defence, as you request, to identify any issues which they intend to raise which they consider do go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief or the credibility of the witness which are permitted. And I hope they will do that now before we make progress and before the witness returns to court. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to make an observation that I -- it seems to me should be rather obvious. What we all have is this diary of notes that were made by this witness. We all have it. It was given to all of us. And the issue seems to be -- we're here in closed session, you know, so this isn't going outside this room. The issue seems to be whether we can share the information in here with you or not. That seems to be the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's not the objection. The objection is that there is a rule here, whether we like it or not, restricting cross-examination to areas explored in examination-in-chief and credibility, and that's credibility in the widest sense; reliability, for example, would fall within that. So if you want to go into territory that can't be related to the examination-in-chief, you need the authority of the Rule 70 provider. And you're being offered it -- I mean, there's a genuine attempt being made, as I understand it, to cooperate so that we don't need to bring the witness back and these additional issues can be explored, but they need to be notified and it may be authority has to be obtained --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to allow them to be explored. So don't assume that just because it's in material that you've been given that it can be explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I accept that and I understand that. But really we are in closed session, and the concern of the Rule 70 provider must be that this material not be made publicly available for whatever reason they want to assign to that. And now that we're in closed session and we do have this material and we're all familiar with it, sitting over here on this side of the courtroom as well as everybody on that side of the courtroom, maybe it makes sense for me to request right now that the Rule 70 provider simply permit us to cross-examine regarding matters contained within these notes without getting into some very heavy specific identification of which ones we want to talk about. And then if there is one that comes up that is particularly bothersome to them, we can certainly take the time to deal with it. But otherwise we're going to have all kinds of problems this afternoon trying to get through this. Because I have several questions that I think are arguably perhaps outside the decision that you have made regarding the scope of cross-examination but are extremely important to doing justice in this case because they go to the heart of matters that are before you. So that's -- that's where I think we are and maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, since the time has passed where you can lose the element of surprise, why don't you communicate as we are continuing just now any that you can identify by reference to the pages and see if a quick decision can be made on whether authority has to be obtained from somewhere else. The fact that we're in closed session does not resolve this. We are faced with a decision by a Rule 70 provider that we have no authority to modify, having made the final decision we did make in deciding that the evidence would be conducted this way. So it's not going to be in anyone's interest to try and circumvent that, except to the extent that we have this offer of cooperation which everyone should make use of, if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, please, Mr. Ackerman try and identify the ones that you think are going to fall outside the area, and we will see if we can get a quick decision on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting right now is that I think the Rule 70 restriction was based on the proposition that we would be in open session. And if in fact that's the case and they're perfectly willing to have use bring these matters to your attention in private session, in closed session like this that are in this document that we all have, they could say so and we could all save time; otherwise, I could sit here and send an e-mail to the Prosecution with each particular page that I'm interested in and that's up to Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, does that provide any solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We could not agree to the use of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. So we will proceed on the basis that there will be electronic communication to try to resolve any that appear obvious, and we leave it to you, Mr. Stamp, to intervene when you consider that an inappropriate question is being asked and we'll address that as it happens. Now, please bring Mr. Phillips back to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've dealt with the outstanding matter, Mr. Phillips. We can now proceed with the cross-examination by Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Phillips?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, one brief matter. I notice right before we took the break this morning, you said I was concerned about two events on the 8th and 9th of January that he didn't know about it. In my haste, Your Honour, I should say in my effort to expedite what was going on this morning, truly an effort to expedite, I did have entries for the 8th and 9th. Everything I've asked about, Your Honour, is indeed contained in his notebooks. And just for the record it's 3D550, pages 3100 for January 8th and page 3104 for January 9th. It's just that we've had some testimony on that before; and in an effort to expedite the trial, Your Honour, and to save time, I asked him whether he had a memory on it, and I think I mislead Your Honour and that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, I believe, Colonel, when we broke, I was about to ask you or had asked you if you could look at 3D550, which refers to a meeting of 10 January 1999, and it says: "Meeting with Sainovic at top of the hour."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher could put that up, please. 3D550, page 3108.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And, first of all -- again, was that a meeting with -- who was at that meeting? Was it you and Ambassador Walker and Mr. Sainovic, or were there others there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: There were likely others there. I can't recall exactly, but I know Ambassador Walker was there, myself was there, Mr. Sainovic was there, and I honestly can't remember who would have been with Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this says, at the fourth paragraph, there: "KLA conducted another ambush near Pec this morning and killed one MUP." And who was saying that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't be accurate there, but I would venture to say probably Mr. Walker. You know, we were -- we shared both events, whether it be the Serbs or the KLA, evenly in those meetings. So I would say Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And was it Mr. Walker who also uttered the next sentence, that is to say: "The KLA is clearly outside their box, and it is impeding their chances for a successful outcome and hurting any chance of putting any real leverage on the Serbs. Urosevic (east of Prizren) ambush, one MUP killed." Was that Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would say that was probably DZ, because he used that terminology "out of their bo" often, so he was probably with us at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So DZ is saying the KLA is just out of the box on this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Down at the bottom of this Exhibit 3D550, it says: "Walker talked with Wes Clark." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it says: "Very worried" by the way, who is very worried? Walker or Clark? "Very worried the press is playing this" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, that area we object to with respect to being outside the scope of the examination-in-chief. A conversation between Wes Clark and Walker were not within the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if we discover that this is something Walker said, you would say that that's outwith the scope of cross-examination? Because the reference to Clark is incidental.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is outside the scope. The examination-in-chief dealt with the meetings in respect to the various accused and another named participator in the joint criminal enterprise as alleged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is a meeting with Sainovic? You're just going to pick and choose the meetings with Sainovic you want to lead evidence about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If it is a meeting with Sainovic, it would be within the scope and I'm willing to be guided. This does not appear to me to be a meeting with Sainovic; if it is, I concede that to be within the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Phillips, is the record at the bottom of this page made in connection with the meeting with Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what connection was it made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this was a phone call Ambassador Walker made back at his office after our meetings with Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're recording what Walker said, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your comment on the objection, Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, for one thing, Your Honour, I wanted to first explore what it meant. It says: "Very worried that the press is playing this" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What does it mean? It looks here as if they're trying to favour Serb forces over the KLA. They don't like it that the KLA is blameworthy on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Deal with the objection that's being taken, that this falls outwith the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, again, I think it has to do with compliance with the agreement -- compliance or not with the agreement. We say the KLA was not in compliance with the agreement, and I think that anything that goes to show that is certainly relevant. And I would direct Your Honours' attention to the statement on the next page, page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It dovetails with this, that's why I mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That would be page 3109. And I ask Your Honours particularly - I won't read- I just say look at the last sentence there at the top of the page, if we can find it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is page 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, right there at the top, and I won't read the sentence, Your Honour. But beginning with the word "our" and ending with the word"Clark. " I think that is a -- that is something that requires explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand you are trying to get things clarified, but the difficulty for us is that if you pick and choose your way through this in this sort of selective way, we don't get an overall picture. And these two entries that Mr. Sepenuk wants to address now are undoubtedly relevant to important issues in this trial. And if we are not allowed to hear evidence about these, then it could well undermine entirely the evidence of this witness to the point where we think it's so unfair to the Defence to prevent them pursuing issues that we have to exclude the evidence completely. Now, we don't want to do that. We've been trying to find a way of achieving the result where we hear the important evidence of a witness so closely involved in these events. There is possible substance in your argument this time, but in the end of the day you could be greatly prejudicing the Prosecution case by standing on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand this and that is what I'm trying to avoid. What I think may well be a solution is if we -- and the providers are prepared to act upon the suggestion of my friend Mr. Ackerman, that the cross-examination on matters which are in the notebook be permitted even it is not within the scope as long as it is relevant to the issues in the case and as long as the material remains under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be making an order at the end of the evidence about how to deal with whether this will become public or not and it will give you time to consider the situation. Obviously we want evidence to be public if possible even though held in closed session, but we will not make an order to that effect here without consideration being given to the evidence as a whole. In the past there have been conditions insisted upon by Rule 70 providers requiring postponement of the publication of the evidence until it was reviewed, obviously, for issues that might affect national security interests or other important interests of the provider. So your position is that the material in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Kept by the witness is open for exploration?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. That's very cooperative and helpful. Thank you very much. Please continue then, Mr. Sepenuk. You may ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We should go back to the prior page and that's 3108, 3D550, 3108. Just highlight the bottom, please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, Colonel, the notation is: "Walker talked with Wes Clark." And the first sentence says: "Very worried the press is playing this as the KLA is to blame because it undercuts his NATO authority." Now, first of all, is this Mr. Walker who is speaking now?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you are taking these notes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So Mr. Walker said that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And can you assist us in determining what Ambassador Walker meant by that comment?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Essentially that -- to frame this is that the KLA is not in compliance with the agreement, with the cease-fire actions that we were to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And how does that undercut General Clark's NATO authority?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, I think that the KLA felt that they were being persecuted to such a point that NATO would come to their rescue, and the fact that the KLA was continuing these aggressive actions didn't make it easy for NATO to make a decision to enter forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It makes it less of a good case for NATO to intervene or to bomb or whatever; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then it says: "The French are playing this to their advantage." Can you explain what Ambassador Walker meant by that or may have meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Within our mission we had Ambassador Walker and Ambassador Kellerman I believe was his name; the French Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was it Keller?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah, Ambassador Keller. And he was very pro-Serb and looked after the Serbs, and I think he was certainly worried that the French had a bid on this. Ambassador Keller had made some phone calls back to Vienna about this and back to his home country, which most of these leadership -- most of the senior leaders and deputies within OSCE did regularly. And Ambassador Walker and Ambassador Keller didn't see eye to eye on the activities going on in Kosovo. So it appeared that when the KLA did something bad, that played well for the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So they didn't -- Ambassador Walker and Ambassador Keller did not see eye to eye?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Ambassador Keller was pro-Serb and Ambassador Walker was what? Anti-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say he was anti-Serb. I think -- over time, I think the bias became more declared that Walker saw the Albanian people more persecuted. But I think that we went in on the ground when we first got there on 4 November very -- very even on the ground on what we thought about the events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And perhaps I misunderstood you. You said over time --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- general Walker -- Ambassador Walker became of the view that the Albanians were being persecuted?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then the last statement is: "Our KVM statements did not help our NATO card with Clark." What's that all about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Essentially, leverage. It was difficult for NATO to use the threat of force under the circumstances of the KLA behaviour and noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So General Clark was unhappy that his sort of master plan was being messed up here. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't know that he was unhappy. I didn't see his, you know -- all I can tell you is that this wasn't going obviously as he needed, to be able to use NATO as leverage to force compliance by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then at the bottom of that page, it says: "KLA command and control structure," and this is, again, of course is Ambassador Walker; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It says: "They are organising these other ambushes," and that means KLA?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: "They are organising these other ambushes to show that they have capability elsewhere and will implement whatever force necessary if Serbs take aggressive action and don't release the eight VJs." By the way, is that right, the eight VJs or does that mean eight KLAs?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Eight KLAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Because this had to do with this prisoner exchange and whatnot?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But, again, that's Ambassador Walker saying that, saying they're organising other ambushes to show that they had this capability?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then if you look -- I'm coming to the end of your notebook, at 3D551, page 3151. And that's 12 February 1999, a meeting with Lieutenant-General, is it, Nicolai Zlenko, Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall that individual, that meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But probably the Russian Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on the next page is what I really wanted to ask you about, it's 3D551, page 3152. And do you recall, by the way, that this is during the time of the Rambouillet conference, February 12th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe it was. And this is general -- this is Ambassador Walker speaking at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he says: "The KLA is a well-trained, well-disciplined guerilla force."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So at least by the time of the Rambouillet conference that was his opinion of the KLA; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And now the last entry that I'm going to ask you about in your notebook is 3D551 at page 3164. And I'm interested in the part with Congressman Wolfe?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If you move it up, please, to the usher, a little bit more, a more yet, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Congressman Wolfe, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Obviously, from the United States Congress, but I don't recall him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. But he had a chat with Ambassador Walker; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So according to this what you've written down, Ambassador Walker -- he's asked a question: "KLA at a George Washington." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And he says, you tell me if I'm wrong, this is what he says: "Some are reasonable." Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And: "Some see themselves as protective force for the Albanians." Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And: "Some resort to terrorism to further their aims." Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But the second thing, which I didn't read and which I read to you now, says: "Greater respect for KLA than VJ MUP." What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think Ambassador Walker refers to that as having the access that he needs and the persuasion that he needs to talk to the KLA. They do listen -- they did listen to him, they did show a restraint for him, and he seemed to take on a better relationship with them when it came to hard political or operational kinds of issues. Ambassador Walker never felt he had that same level of trust in the relationship with the VJ or the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And your testimony -- what you just said is that they did show grate restraint with him. After what we've just heard today, is that called great restraint by you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The way you've presented, which is as a KLA view of this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Great restraint by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And that's the last entry that we have for your notebook, and, again, as I understand it, the notebook for the next month is either lost or misplaced. In any event, we have no access to it, and I take it you don't either?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So -- but you did -- you were there for the next month, correct? You were there from -- the last entry was February 16th, and you were there until March 20, 21, somewhere in there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: March 20th, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you were observing the scene --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- with Ambassador Walker? You're getting reports from the -- your mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And reading them and absorbing them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And following the Rambouillet conference, I want to ask you whether you agree or not with statement that General DZ said in this court, a statement that he submitted. He said: "I must say that during the Rambouillet discussions, the number of incidents instigated by the Serbs declined significantly; whereas, those instigated by the KLA declined much less appreciably. Furthermore, the KLA became more opportunistic during this time." Does this jive with your recollection, too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. That does fall outwith. The question is whether you're going to allow it or not. The Rambouillet negotiations played no part in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It does fall outside, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Move on to something else, Mr. Sepenuk, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. This could be the end of my cross-examination then, because I just wanted for the sake of the record, though, Your Honour, say that I had a number of questions dealing with matters that happened after the Rambouillet negotiations and reports by KVM on KLA atrocities against civilians, Albanian, and Serb civilians, against the MUP. I have notes from DZ that I was going to show him which talk about widespread violations by the KLA of agreements. And, finally, I have a report of 21 March 1999 which talks about KLA killings and terrorism in the Pristina area, and that would have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what would have been your purpose in raising these issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Again, showing that the -- it was the KLA which had an increased level of provocation, and that that's what the Serbs were responding to. The Serbs were responding to this increased KLA provocation, and for that they were bombed. That's our argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's the purpose, then you don't need the contribution of this witness to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, except he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're going to try to challenge what he's been saying, that's different; but if all you're doing is seeking his confirmation to some extent of things that have been proved otherwise or will be proved otherwise in this case, it's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I can -- if Your Honours feel that it indeed has been proven, we respectfully submit that it has, but that's for Your Honours to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I perhaps overstated it, but can be proved by other evidence and may indeed be proved by other evidence so far. It doesn't seem that you're really challenging the witness in any respect that requires you to present him with all this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, this is all elicited for the benefit of the Trial Chamber; and, of course, if that's the feeling of the Trial Chamber, I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Equally, since it does fall outwith what you're permitted to do today, you have the opportunity of raising it with the Rule 70 provider in seeking authority, and it looks as though we'll have the witness tomorrow. So as we indicated in our order at the time, we hoped that you would deal with this request quickly to try to get the authority and complete the witness at one go. So you can reflect on that, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before Mr. Ackerman proceeds, there is another procedural difficulty. There's an order in respect to the notification of the exhibits, and we have received an exhibit -- a notification from Mr. Ackerman which -- which does not refer to the Defence exhibit numbers as would be reflected in e-court, which I think is what the order of the Court indicates should be done. There are just four-digit numbers here in this notification, so we are not in a position to follow where these exhibits are from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can assume that each one should be preceded by P00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no idea what Mr. Stamp is talking about. I haven't notified them about any exhibits that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that there is an order that the Defence should tell us the exhibit numbers of the exhibits they intend to use during cross-examination, and the order was that they should be transmitted at the time the cross-examination begins. This was not transmitted at the time the cross-examination begun, firstly; secondly, which is the gravaman of the point. The exhibit numbers are not here. This is an e-mail that says: "Here are the area and page numbers to which I wish to refer," and a list -- a long list of numbers. This is not in accordance of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand what's going on. You asked me to communicate to them by e-mail the page numbers I wanted to use for the Rule 70, which I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're all from the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They're all from the notebook. It has nothing to do with your prior order, and I have no intention of using any exhibits during cross-examination, not any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a with request for authority to go into that territory from the notebooks, and you've since superseded it by saying that that's permissible since we're in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I was expressing my gratitude to being told what it is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as long as we're into expressing gratitude, let me express mine to my American colleagues that are here today for responding rather quickly to my request that I be allowed to go into this matter. I think that was generous, and I will be extremely careful; and if at any time my American colleagues want to object to anything I'm doing, I certainly will welcome that because I don't want to open up any matters that would cause any embarrassment to my government. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The questions I'm going to be asking you today, as I have indicated, are going to refer almost exclusively to your diary and the entries in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like the usher to come bring you this book, because this actually has all the pages of that diary that I'll be referring to and more. I haven't put any of the pages in to the e-court system, because I didn't intend to make any of them an exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- if my friend, Mr. Ackerman, would also identify which diary, which months, so that we can also follow quickly here as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As I ask the questions and I have given him every month that you have given me, Mr. Stamp, so this book contains his entire diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does that mean, Mr. Ackerman, that this is being used as an aide-memoire and is not an exhibit in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is not an exhibit in the case. I just want to be fair to the witness so he can check what I'm suggesting what appears in his diary, if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it makes any sense to make it an exhibit because they're minor little matters -- I shouldn't call them minor, but they're small matters that I want to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this probably is a small matter. If we start -- you'll see that I've divided it into tabs, Colonel, and we start with tab 1. And then the page numbers I'm referring to are the page numbers you see up in the upper right-hand corner of the document. So when I refer to tab 1, page 6767, you should be able to find that rather quickly because those ERN numbers, we call them, are fairly large up in the upper left -- right-hand corner of the document there. And the page I'm referring to actually also has a page number, 18. And this is apparently some notes you made during a fairly extensive meeting that was held on November 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Another point arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's just a request for better directions. I know it's tabbed in that record which he has handed to the witness, but there are so many documents for us to find that we need the month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have another copy of that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because it is your obligation to give the Prosecutor notice of the material you're going to be using, whether it's in e-court or not, and it's going to be difficult for Mr. Stamp to follow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it is. I think it's going to be pretty easy when I explain to him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. But bear in mind it's not just exhibits that need to be notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I did notify them that I would be using this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And for the Prosecution's information, each of the tabs is a specific segment of the diary that was provided by the Prosecutor, and I've simply arranged them in chronological order so that tab 1 would be the first one and tab 2 would be the one that begins with the next date in order, which would be 21 November. And I assume that probably matches the way they have them arranged. It would make sense to arrange them that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can help, Your Honour, that would be P2840 in the bunchings that the Prosecution did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no idea what that means either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's continue now, Mr. Ackerman, with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you can find where we are at page 6767. It took a long time to get to a question that probably doesn't make a lot of difference. It was just a matter of curiosity. I was wondering why you wrote in there: "Ugly CNN moments are buried in this." Do you have any idea what that means?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That comment had to do with if Ambassador Walker was responsible for all the verifiers that were in Kosovo, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wish the evidence was thorough, and I am not being obstructive. We can't find it based on what is being represented by my friend. I am just trying to find a way that we can go through it smoothly. The documents -- there are ten separate notebook extracts that were put into the system and disclosed to the Defence. Perhaps if Mr. Ackerman could refer to the ERN numbers of each extract or of each batch he wants to use, that might assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, that's what I'm doing. I told the witness I was referring to page 6767. Now, if you want, I can also say it's 03216767, but I don't think that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I was asking for is the ERN range for each batch of those ten documents, but if we get the first date for each --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we put the documents on the ELMO, one by one, as you're referring to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's going to take us forever, Judge, and I can do this really fast. This will go a lot faster than putting them on the ELMO, I guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have to be fair to your opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is what I am doing. I am going to give him what he just asked for. Tab 1 is 03216750; tab 2 is 03224998; tab 3 is 03216702; tab 4, 03224958; tab 5, 03216661; tab 6, 03216626; tab 7, 03216582; tab 8, 03224924; tab 9, 03216535; tab 10, 03224892. I have to repeat the first three, Your Honour: Tab 1 is 03216750; tab 2, 03224998; tab 3, 03216702 [Realtime transcript read in error "03216705"]. Your Honour, I deliberately chose to use ERN numbers because those are the numbers the Prosecution uses to identify documents, and I apparently have confused them to no end by using their own identification system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that last one 705 or 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was -- I don't know what you mean by the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tab 3 I think you said it finished 702, but it's come up on the transcript as 705.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just wonder if that has assisted my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That will be okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Colonel, I think we're going to finally get going here. You were trying to put the mission together, and you determined the tasks that were to be performed by your mission. There was some uncertainty about those tasks, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there was a perceived need to try to get some kind of an agreement with Milosevic about the parameters of the mission. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you actually made a note of that at page 6768. You don't need to look at it unless you feel the need to. At page 6774, you describe the agreement you were trying to deal with as "severely fragmented" and "there is room for interpretation by Milosevic." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then if we go over to tab 2, go to page 5036 of that tab, you'll see that Walker even commented to Reuters about this, and he said on 29 November 1998: "We read the agreements in the broadest of terms, while the FRY views it in the narrowest of terms." Right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you wrote it because it's what Walker said?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, before the creation of your OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission, there was this prior mission there called KDOM, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during their mission, they had acquired a great deal of information of various kinds that would be helpful to the KVM mission that was coming in to take their place basically?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if not just helpful, maybe even crucial to a successful beginning of that mission, and certainly one that would give it a running start. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these earlier KDOM missions were divided among, I think, if I've not got this wrong, the UK-KDOM, the US-KDOM, the EU-KDOM, and the Russian KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And each of those had a responsibility for a particular portion of the province of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Is that a question or just a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I can speed things up by not putting "isn't that true" on the end of each question, if you'll understand my statements as being a question to you and see if we can move faster. And you did have some difficulty with that because - and you'll find this in tab 1, 6783 - the US-KDOM would not turn their information over to you, and they said that was because of a directive from Washington not to do so. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: On early going, there was some what I would call turf battles on how this was going to be arranged. That's a correct statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume that all finally got ironed out and straightened out?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 6796, just a little further - and I don't know if this is related to that turf battle or something else - there's an entry 14 November 1998, and you've got the number 1600 there. What's that number, 1600, mean? Was that the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dick Holbrooke and Ambassador Walker going to Milosevic, and you make the note: "Chris Hill believed that DC is overreacting. Feels not quite as desperate as Washington feels." What was that, if you recall, what he believed Washington was overreacting to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall what that leads to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. On the next page, 13 November 1998, apparently, there was a meeting going on with Shaun Byrnes, and you make a notation there that Walker is to be "dual-hatted." We know one of those hats was his position with the KVM mission. What was the other one?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Just permit me to look through here just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, although we have agreed to the general use of that notebook, some of these questions, the last one in particular, are directed to areas which are well outside the issues before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. This is 13th November, which is a period the witness has given evidence about and the arrival of himself as Chief of Staff to Walker on the scene, and this seem set the scene and we're trying to get the overall picture, I think, and that seems to me to fall within the territory we explored in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- on the page I'm looking at, on page 48, I do not see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, my advice is that -- my instructions are that these -- this area refers to matters which are not permissible which the provider will not permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'd withdraw the objections, and I regret the delayed interruption to my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was just getting ready to give up on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer to the dual-hatted question. The dual-hatting was only an interim fix for Ambassador Walker to take on the KDOM mission and its personnel and the KVM mission at the same time until they were merged as one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So was there a point when Walker was actually in charge of KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would tell you no. Shaun Byrnes and the State Department held close to KDOM. It was the intent, but it never really materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I seriously doubt that KDOM would have done anything at the direction of Ambassador Walker. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't make a judgement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to tab 2 at 5015, and I think you do need to look at it to respond to my question. It's a 24 November 1998 entry, and it begins with apparently a meeting with Shaun Byrnes. And while we've gotten to this point, let me digress a moment and go back to a matter that came up this morning, and that was a meeting that you said you had with Milosevic on this date, 24 November 1998. Now, the first thing that we'll just recollect for the record is that the letter that was sent to Milosevic was dated 23 November 1998, which was the day before this date that we see here on page 5014. And at page 7, line 9 of your testimony this morning, you told us that you and Walker delivered that letter to Milosevic on the 24th. And at page 8, line 1, you described a heated meeting with Milosevic at that time, where he became very loud and upset. Now, if we look at a page that I've got you looking at right now, that's your first November 24th entry, we certainly see some of the things that happened that day. You had this meeting with Shaun Byrnes. There was apparently a phone call from Dick Holbrooke at 2.48 in the afternoon. You talk about a meeting with Hill and Milosevic. You talk about a call you made to Loncar's people. And then when you go over on to the second page -- actually, it's page 5018, and this is where I get confused. At 5018, you say this -- this is in the dinner with Sainovic that night: "The letter we sent to Milosevic explains what we were verifying." You say: "It went out on Wednesday, 25 November," and what I'm wondering is if you actually discussed this letter with Mr. Milosevic on the 24th, why you say it didn't go out until the next day, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah, all good points. I'm clearly confused with the dates. We met with Milosevic. We delivered a letter to him that made him upset. You know, I'll have to go back and look at the dates, but even now I'm confused now on what that date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look -- if we go to tab 3 now and look at 6709, this is a -- I think this all deals with a ministerial meeting of the OSCE, which I think was in Vienna on the 2nd and 3rd of December. And there's point where Ambassador Walker makes a speech at that meeting, basically reporting on how things were going. And one of the things he mentions, if you look on page 6709: "Met with Milosevic, friendly." Now, I assume the only meeting he can be talking about is the one where you delivered this letter, where you say that Milosevic was very upset and yelling and making a lot of noise and not friendly, but why does Mr. Walker then explain it to the OSCE ministers as being a friendly meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, there were several meetings. Ambassador Walker I think attended probably four. I was with him on probably three. The meeting where we expressed to Mr. Milosevic that we did not see full and unfettered access and cooperation was one where he was upset, and that was a letter that was personally delivered to him from Mr. Walker. There was another letter that was written that outlined an understanding of the agreement, and my recollection was that that was also delivered in person to Mr. Milosevic. But it came with Ambassador Miles from the US consulate. Whoever hand -- I'm not certain who actually handed it to him, but I -- but, you know, the meeting where we discussed Serb cooperation was the meeting where Mr. Milosevic was upset. He felt that he was cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this speech to the OSCE ministers was like ten days after the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there wasn't any meeting with Milosevic between the 24th of November and the 2nd or 3rd of December, was there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't recall. I have to certainly look at my notes and see, but I know we had a couple of meetings certainly before Christmas with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to go back to where I was to start with, if you go over to -- back to page 5014.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: What tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: What tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, that's tab 2. That's that first entry of 24 November, a meeting with Shaun Byrnes. If you just turn the page to 5015, the heading is: "Holbrooke talk." Was Holbrooke there? Was he talking there or was this a phone call or what was this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would tell you that this was a phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's probably the case because you refer to a phone call from Holbrooke at 1448 on the prior page. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Holbrooke wanted the Byrnes-Hill-Walker team to work more closely together, and I believe, you know, one of his concerns was, you know, sitting down together and looking where there were -- where there was opportunity for good solid political solutions between both parties on the Serb and the Albanian side. Ambassador Hill was fairly independent coming into Kosovo and not making a time in all cases to speak with Ambassador Walker or Mr. Shaun Byrnes, and I think it was more a push by Holbrooke to pull this team together and do so more teaming on what we were trying to accomplish there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Move ahead a little bit to page 5023; and if you look at 5022, it's 26 November 1998, the Belgian Ambassador is apparently paying you a visit. And apparently Walker had a meeting with him and you have indicated some of the things that Walker was telling the Belgian ambassador. And if we look at that page 5023, you say this: "On the issue of compliance, Milosevic has a legitimate reason to be upset by the action of the KLA. They are taking advantage of the fire. It is a valid complaint by the FRY government." Now, that was the situation on the ground on 26 November when Ambassador Walker was meeting with the Belgian Ambassador, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a -- that was the ambassador from Belgium's comment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was his comment?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume Walker agreed with that. I don't see any disagreement from you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall whether he agreed with it or not. At this point in the mission, I would think that he probably would have agreed, but it's just conjecture on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, for -- I want to ask you something now that maybe is a little bit sensitive, and I'm going to state a assumption. And if you feel free to agree with me, you may; and if you rather not answer the question, that would be okay with me, too. There's an indication in tab 3 at 6711 that there was -- and you find this more than one place in your diaries. It had to do with some dispute about whether the Russians would have access to your fusion centre or not. And the assumption that I make about that is that it was a NATO concern regarding the security of NATO information. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Would you feel comfortable telling us what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. I don't think it's an area which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't immediately strike me as relevant, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, that's why I was cautious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you were very cautious. Thank you. We can pass over it then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Keep going to page 6723, and this is, if you look at 6721, a 3 December 1998 meeting with number two. Who would number two be?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Where is that statement again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's on page 6721 is the beginning of the entry, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just, without objecting, I don't know the answer to that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- and I would ask the witness be advised that if the answer would reveal sources which are confidential that he indicate so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I imagine Mr. Phillips is well-trained in identifying what ought and ought not to be disclosed, and I leave it to you, Mr. Phillips, in a situation like this to tell us if there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can't comment on that particular entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will withdraw my question about who number two is, and ask you to go to page 6723 and there is a note there. I don't know whether it's yours or something this number two person told you. Michael O'Connor, who we've heard earlier about from the New York Times, says: "The UCK is moving/oozing back into areas they once owned, so yes they may have a tackle advantage at this point." So that was 3 December 1998. Was that the situation at that point?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would tell you yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had some conversation with Mr. Sepenuk earlier today about an entry that begins on page 6729, which is called "NAC with SecGen." You explained that was a NATO group and Secretary-General was Solana. The part of that that I'm interested in is page 6734 where you make the notation: "Both sides," I assume that means the Serbs and the KLA,"seemed to want international community to see them in a good light." I assume that was an observation that Walker is making or certainly that someone in that meeting is making, and I assume also that you accept and agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was a comment by Mr. Walker, and I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, we're going to go to tab 4 now, and that tab begins with a 9 -- a report of a 9 December 1998 meeting with Sainovic. And if you go over to page 4963, we get to a matter that Mr. Sepenuk dwelled on just briefly. Mr. Sainovic is complaining that money in western Europe that was frozen to keep the KLA from buying arms had been released and was no longer frozen, and that that was a problem and asked Walker to try to deal with it; and then you'll see where Walker responds to that, and he says this: "I will speak to the international community about providing money to buy arms is a no-go. Bank assets need to be re-frozen. I do not want the KLA buying more or better weapons. I will do something about this. We will do everything in our power to stop the flow of arms." That's what Walker told Mr. Sainovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your view, was he being honest with Sainovic at that point or was he feeding him some kind of a --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was sincere with Mr. Sainovic, as Mr. Sainovic was with Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't answer my question. Was he being sincere?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I just said he was being sincere with Mr. Sainovic, as Mr. Sainovic was being sincere with him during this portion of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That still doesn't answer the question. The only way I could know what your answer is if I know how sincere Mr. Sainovic was being?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: And I've already stated in testimony that he was sincere in his cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not put as a comparison, Mr. Ackerman, it's "I just said he was being," not as sincere, "but sincere with Mr. Sainovic, as Sainovic was being with him."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I misunderstood it, Your Honour, and I'm satisfied with the answer and I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we go 12 days down the road and look under tab 5 at page 6684, this is 21 December 1998, and there is a notation regarding an Ambassador Jim Pardue at the bottom of page 6684. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was Ambassador Jim Pardue?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was a State Department official who was making a visit to Kosovo at the time. He was the State Department official who looked after the activities in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there's nothing about Ambassador Walker saying to Pardue, Well, I promised Sainovic that we were going to cut off the money flow several days ago, and we need to do that without with regard to what they're doing because I made that promise to Sainovic. I don't see that in your notes. Did Walker tell him that he made that promise?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker did bring the issue up with Ambassador Pardue and also with the OSCE in Vienna that this needed to cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go to tab 6, now we're at 27 December 1998, and this is Ambassador Walker's interview with Mike O'Connor of the New York Times and --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: What number -- page number there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page number 6632 under tab 6. And apparently Mike O'Connor asks Ambassador Walker: "What are you going to do if the KLA kills one of us? And Walker says: "Declare them terrorists, use the press, interfere with their arms supply and bank accounts." So he's still saying, you know, we will do that in the future, even though he's promised Sainovic that he would absolutely do that several days ago now; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It makes sense, yes. I would just tell you, you know, Ambassador Walker did not have the wherewithal to reach in and turn off those spigots. He had to go back to the Contact Group for that help and OSCE in Vienna for that help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's absolutely the case, and it may very well be that Ambassador Walker wanted to accomplish that and was unable to. I certainly wouldn't want to suggest anything else, but it does seem that he was unable to get that done even though he promised Sainovic he would for whatever reason. I take it you don't know what reason he was unable to get that done?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now we're going to go back to tab 4, and it's page 4982 of your diary. And this is a situation that was discussed with you just a little bit by Mr. Sepenuk earlier today. Now, this describes the situation where the Panda Bar incident occurred and the KLA were ambushed along the border coming across the border, and this was really the first major incident that came up during your mission in Kosovo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I missed a portion of your question as I was trying to read through the text. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're talking about a situation here on the 14th of December and over into the 15th, where there had been a -- an ambush of some KLA coming across the border into Kosovo and several of them had been killed in that ambush; and then the next thing that happened is what is described on the next page, 4983, as a retaliatory strike in a Serb bar, that would be the Panda Bar, where a number of young Serb children, I'll say, were killed and several more were wounded. I think six were killed and 15 were wounded. And my question is: This basically was the first major incident that came up during your mission there and attracted a great deal of concern.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: You know, we landed on the 4th of November. This was a big issue, I remember that, I couldn't tell you if it was the first big issue. It depends on how you define that, but this incident here was a major concern for Ambassador Walker and we were very unhappy about it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, somewhere in your diary, and I won't be able to find it now, you did make a list of major things that had happened and this is one of them?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't dispute that, but I just can't put it in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not terribly important. What I really do want to ask you about is a reaction from Holbrooke that you'll find --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move on to that, Your Honour, since we are not exhibiting this document, just to be accurate, the retaliatory strike which my friend refers to, the document says four dead, seven wounded. I think he said it the other way around, seven dead, four wounded or something like that, Just to be accurate for the record, it says four dead, seven wounded -- or the notebook says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's true that the note says that and there's a later note which updates it to seven dead and 15 wounded. And I'll find that if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, proceed to your last question now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're on page 4990, Colonel, and this is I think a reaction to this situation that developed there on the 14th, where apparently there's some communication with Holbrooke in which Holbrooke says, according to your note: "I'm in favour of bringing NATO ground troops. NATO does favour an international security force to come into Kosovo. We have only 14 weeks." I don't know what "only 14 weeks" means. Maybe you do and maybe you don't. I'd like you to tell me if you do. It looks like Holbrooke is reacting to this as a basis for bringing in NATO troops already at this point.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The discussion on NATO troops entering Kosovo was predicated on the fact that the OSCE verifiers were unarmed, and it was felt that if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the question really invites the witness to enter into an area of NATO policy which is way outside of not just the scope but of his personal knowledge. It really invites him to speculate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is something the witness heard said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, he heard it, but this is speaking about NATO policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I'm not sure if there could -- if my friend could go beyond confirming that this is what he heard said, but for the witness to comment on how policies formulated in NATO is well beyond anything that he would know personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he wants an explanation on what the 14 weeks was a reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if that is the end to all of the question, but I don't know if that's the way the question was phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, pretty much, Your Honour, and the witness has been quite good at telling me if there are matters that he doesn't have knowledge of and can't comment on, so I'm not worried about him going into something he doesn't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know what the 14 weeks referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you tell Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When spring arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was concern about there being a spring offensive?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that it for today, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think so, Mr. Ackerman. I'm afraid you need to come back, Mr. Phillips, because that's the end of our time for today. It's just not feasible to sit on any longer even to deal with one individual witness. So we need you at 9.00 tomorrow morning. It's very important that you have no discussion with anyone about any aspect of your evidence, either the evidence you've already given or the evidence you may yet give. So overnight speak to whoever you like about whatever you like as long as you do not discuss the evidence and it's important -- particularly important in your case, as I explained earlier, because there are representatives of your government in court and the restriction applies to them as well. If there is any need for them to speak to you, then they would apply to the Court for permission to do so. So could you leave the court now with the usher and be back to resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I asked that you come into court to deal with one particular question for us in relation to your application, the second one, for the admission of exhibits from the bar table. And one of these exhibits is 1378 which is described as a transcript of an interview from PBS Frontline. It's been obtained from a web site. Your request doesn't indicate what it is or anything else about its provenance. Can you help us on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm advised that Frontline is a TV programme. This was a Frontline TV documentary programme special on the Kosovo conflict and there were interviews of several of the key players. I don't know if Your Honour were aware. We had also, I think, a Frontline interview of General Clark included in the materials we disclosed in connection with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can give you the web site address from which it was downloaded. Mr. Coo actually downloaded it from the web site I think some years ago when he first wrote his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but was the interview actually broadcast on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's that information that we would like. Having looked at it, it just appears as questions and answers on a web site and it really doesn't tell any more than it's something to do with Frontline but whether they simply put it on the web or whether they actually broadcast it, we would be interested to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll see if I can find out whether the entire thing was broadcast or portions of it were broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's also important to know the extent to which there's been editing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will obtain all the available information on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First thing tomorrow morning if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have already ruled if we were to use any material from a couple of BBC documentaries, that we had to have them properly translated by CLSS. And I think it's very clear that this has not translated by CLSS. We have no idea who -- now, General Pavkovic does not speak English so his answers would have been in Serbian and they would have been translated, if he in fact, gave that interview, I think he probably did, but in any event we have no idea who translated it and what the accuracy of that translation might be, so I think that's another basis for excluding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that does have to be addressed. I had assumed after reading it that it was an interview conducted in English but that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can't happen because he speaks no English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This does require then further investigation, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
